terraflux.io.load_raster.name: load_raster
terraflux.io.load_raster.sig:
load_raster(
    source,
    *,
    band: int | Iterable[int] | None = None,
    masked: bool | str = 'auto',
    chunks: Any = None,
    validate: str | None = None,
    like=None,
    resampling: str = 'auto',
    clip=None,
    stack: bool = False,
    errors: str = 'raise',
    recursive: bool = False,
)
terraflux.io.load_raster.summary: Read one raster, or collect many.

doc.x:
One function for every raster terraflux reads: habitat and land-cover
maps, continuous surfaces, species stacks, costs. The result is a
georeferenced ``xarray.DataArray`` (CRS, transform and NoData via
``.rio``) that [`write_raster()`][terraflux.write_raster] writes back as it was.

i:
One raster (path or GDAL URL), a directory (its ``.tif``/``.tiff``
files), a glob pattern (``"tiles/*.tif"``) or a list of any of these.

Bands to read (1-based): ``None`` (default) reads them all, an integer
one band, a list several. One band gives a ``(y, x)`` array, several a
``(band, y, x)`` array whose ``band`` coordinate holds the band
descriptions when every band has a distinct one (else the band
numbers). Several rasters: each file must have one band, or give
``band=N``.

NoData handling. ``"auto"`` (default): in floating-point rasters NoData
becomes NaN; integer rasters (class maps) keep their codes, with the
NoData value in ``.rio.nodata``, so they are not turned into floats.
``True``: NoData becomes NaN in every raster (integers become
``float32``, or ``float64`` for 32- and 64-bit integers). ``False``: the
values as stored.

Single raster only: ``None`` (default) loads the data into memory;
anything else (e.g. ``"auto"``) returns a lazy dask-backed array.

``"mspa"`` checks that the map is an MSPA input: ``uint8`` coded
0 = missing, 1 = background, 2 = foreground, with some foreground and
some background. ``None`` (default) reads any raster; the
habitat-pattern tools check their input themselves.

A raster (DataArray or path) whose grid the result is put on,
reprojected and resampled when the CRS, resolution or extent differ,
with the coordinates of ``like`` (so that arithmetic between the two
aligns cell by cell). Cells outside the source are NoData. Several
rasters (a list, a folder or a pattern) with ``like`` give one
``(band, y, x)`` stack named by the files, whatever their grids.

With ``like``: ``"auto"`` (default) takes the nearest cell for integer
rasters (classes) and interpolates floats bilinearly; or any GDAL
method: ``"nearest"``, ``"bilinear"``, ``"cubic"``, ``"average"``,
``"mode"``, ``"sum"``, ``"min"``, ``"max"``...

A region (polygons as a GeoDataFrame, GeoSeries or shapely geometries,
or bounds ``(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)`` in the raster's CRS): only the
window of the region is read, the cells outside the polygons are NoData
(see [`clip()`][terraflux.clip]). For a small area of a large raster, reading is
much faster.

Several rasters only: return a lazy ``(file, y, x)`` DataArray (one
dask chunk per file) instead of a [`RasterCollection`][terraflux.RasterCollection]. All
rasters must share the same grid.

Several rasters only: ``"raise"`` (default) if any file is unusable,
``"skip"`` to leave such files out (listed in ``.skipped``).
Several rasters only: also search sub-directories.

For one raster, a georeferenced ``(y, x)`` or ``(band, y, x)`` array.
For several, a [`RasterCollection`][terraflux.RasterCollection] that reads only the file
headers now; pass it to [`mspa()`][terraflux.mspa] to process every raster
in parallel. With ``stack=True``, a lazy DataArray.
If a file does not satisfy the requested checks.
A habitat map (0 missing, 1 background, 2 habitat) and a land-cover map:

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))
>>> forest.shape, str(forest.dtype)
((1000, 1000), 'uint8')
>>> landcover = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc"))
>>> landcover.rio.crs.to_epsg()
3035
On the grid of another raster (here a coarser one in another CRS):
Only a study area, read from a large raster:

>>> x0, y0, x1, y1 = landcover.rio.bounds()
>>> tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc"), clip=(x0, y0, x0 + 10000, y0 + 5000)).shape
(200, 400)
Checked as an MSPA input on reading:
A multi-band stack keeps its band names; NoData of floats is NaN:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import xarray as xr
>>> habitats = xr.concat([landcover.isin([23, 24, 25]), landcover == 41], dim="band").astype("float32")
>>> habitats = habitats.assign_coords(band=["forest", "water"]).where(landcover != 1)  # no data in towns
>>> _ = tf.write_raster(habitats, "stacks/habitats.tif")   # creates the folder
>>> stack = tf.load_raster("stacks/habitats.tif")
>>> stack.dims, stack.band.values.tolist()
(('band', 'y', 'x'), ['forest', 'water'])
>>> bool(stack.sel(band="water").isnull().any()), tf.load_raster("stacks/habitats.tif", band=2).dims
(True, ('y', 'x'))
Many rasters at once (a folder, a pattern or a list) give a collection:

terraflux.io.match_grid.name: match_grid
terraflux.io.match_grid.sig: match_grid(data: xr.DataArray, like, *, resampling: str = 'auto') -> xr.DataArray
terraflux.io.match_grid.summary: Put a raster on the grid of another: same CRS, cells and coordinates.

doc.x:
Rasters from different sources (a species model, a cost layer, a
land-cover map) rarely share their grid; most tools need them cell by
cell. ``match_grid`` reprojects and resamples ``data`` onto the grid of
``like`` with GDAL's resampling (in parallel), and gives it the
coordinates of ``like``. [`load_raster()`][terraflux.load_raster] does the same on reading
with ``like=``, and [`reproject()`][terraflux.reproject] with ``like=`` (which also
reprojects to a CRS, and vectors).

i: Georeferenced ``(y, x)`` or ``(band, y, x)`` DataArray.
The target grid: a DataArray or a raster path.

``"auto"`` (default): nearest cell for integer rasters, bilinear for
floats; or a GDAL method (``"nearest"``, ``"bilinear"``, ``"cubic"``,
``"average"``, ``"mode"``, ``"sum"``...).

``data`` on the grid of ``like``; cells outside ``data`` are NoData
(NaN for floats). A lazy (dask) raster stays lazy.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> landcover = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc"))
>>> coarse = landcover.coarsen(x=4, y=4).mean()          # 100 m instead of 25 m
>>> back = tf.match_grid(coarse, landcover)
>>> back.shape == landcover.shape, bool((back.x == landcover.x).all())
(True, True)

terraflux.io.reclassify.name: reclassify
terraflux.io.reclassify.sig:
reclassify(
    data,
    table=None,
    *,
    foreground: Iterable[int] | int | Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None,
    missing: Iterable[int] | int | None = None,
    background: Iterable[int] | int | None = None,
    others='keep',
    dtype=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
)
terraflux.io.reclassify.summary: Give the values of a raster new values: from a table, or into a habitat map.

doc.x:
**With a table**, every value (or range of values) becomes the value the
table gives it: land-cover classes into resistances or costs, classes
grouped, a continuous map cut into classes. The table is

- a ``dict`` ``{old: new}``; a key may be a range ``(low, high)``;
- a list of pairs ``(old, new)`` or of ranges ``(low, high, new)``, which
  hold the values ``low <= v < high`` (``-np.inf`` / ``np.inf`` for open
  ends); where ranges overlap, the first one wins;
- a DataFrame (e.g. from [`load_table()`][terraflux.load_table]) of two columns (old, new) or
  three (low, high, new), or a 2-D array of the same.

**With** ``foreground`` (or a value, a list of values or a function in place
of the table), the result is a habitat map (0 = missing, 1 = background,
2 = habitat), the input of [`mspa()`][terraflux.mspa], [`fad()`][terraflux.fad] and the other
habitat-pattern tools.

i: Raster: numpy array, DataArray (dask-backed ones stay lazy), any type.

Habitat map: value(s) that become habitat (2), or a function of the
values returning a boolean mask (e.g. ``lambda a: a >= 30`` on a
tree-cover percentage).

Habitat map: value(s) that become missing (0). NaN and the raster's
NoData value are always missing.

Habitat map: value(s) that become background (1). By default every value
that is neither habitat nor missing; when given, the remaining values
become missing.

Table: what values the table does not hold become: ``"keep"`` (default,
their own value), ``"nodata"``, or a number. NoData stays NoData.

Table: output type (default: the smallest that holds the new values, and
the kept ones).
Land-cover classes into resistance to movement (the other classes: 50):

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> landcover = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc"))
>>> resistance = tf.reclassify(landcover, {23: 1, 24: 1, 25: 1, 18: 10, 1: 1000}, others=50)
>>> str(resistance.dtype), sorted(int(v) for v in set(resistance.values.ravel()))
('uint16', [1, 10, 50, 1000])
Ranges of a continuous map into classes, ``[low, high)``:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> footprint = np.array([[0.0, 3.5], [12.0, np.nan]])
>>> tf.reclassify(footprint, [(0, 4, 1), (4, 10, 2), (10, np.inf, 3)])
array([[ 1.,  1.],
       [ 3., nan]])
Forests of a CORINE land-cover map (classes 23, 24 and 25) as a habitat map:

>>> forest = tf.reclassify(landcover, foreground=[23, 24, 25])
>>> sorted(int(v) for v in set(forest.values.ravel()))
[1, 2]
>>> morph = tf.mspa(forest)
A rule on a continuous map, water (class 41) left out as missing:

terraflux.io.write_raster.name: write_raster
terraflux.io.write_raster.sig:
write_raster(
    data,
    path: PathLike,
    *,
    like=None,
    crs=None,
    transform=None,
    nodata=None,
    dtype=None,
    band_names=None,
    colormap: str | dict | None = 'auto',

    description: str | None = None,
    driver: str | None = None,

terraflux.io.write_raster.summary: Write a raster: one band or several, any format GDAL writes.

doc.x:
One function for every raster terraflux writes. It keeps what the data
says about itself (georeferencing, NoData, band names, the colours and
parameters of terraflux's products) and stores it so that GIS software
and [`load_raster()`][terraflux.load_raster] read it back as it was:

- floating-point data with NaN get NaN as NoData (or ``nodata``, which then
  replaces the NaN); integers keep the ``.rio.nodata`` of the data;
- ``bool`` is written as ``uint8`` and 64-bit integers as the smallest
  integer type that holds them;
- GeoTIFFs are compressed with the predictor that suits the type, tiled when
  larger than 512 x 512 and BigTIFF when needed; the format follows the file
  extension (``.tif``, ``.asc``, ``.img``, ``.nc``...) or ``driver``
  (``"COG"``: Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFF);
- dask arrays are written block by block, never whole in memory;
- missing folders of ``path`` are created.

i:
2-D ``(y, x)`` or 3-D ``(band, y, x)`` ``xarray.DataArray``
(georeferencing taken from ``.rio``), numpy or dask array.

A raster (path or DataArray) on the same grid whose CRS and transform
georeference ``data``, e.g. a numpy result computed from an input.

Coordinate reference system and affine transform; they override those of
``data`` and ``like``.

Coordinate reference system and affine transform; they override those of
``data`` and ``like``.

NoData value; overrides the one of ``data``. NaN in the data are written
as this value.

Data type to write (default: the data's, see above). Floats cast to
integers get ``nodata`` (or the type's maximum, minimum if signed) where
they are NaN.

Band descriptions (default: a ``band`` coordinate of strings, e.g. from
[`load_raster()`][terraflux.load_raster]).

``"auto"`` (default) embeds the colour table of the product when ``data``
is a class map made by terraflux (MSPA, fragmentation, change...),
``"mspa"`` forces the MSPA colours, a ``{value: colour}`` mapping (colours
as ``"#rrggbb"``, names or ``(r, g, b[, a])``) embeds your own and ``None``
none. One-band ``uint8``/``uint16`` only.
TIFF image description (MSPA results record their parameters there).
GDAL format (default: from the extension of ``path``).
A terraflux result keeps its colours and parameters:

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))
>>> tf.write_raster(tf.mspa(forest), "forest_mspa.tif").name
'forest_mspa.tif'
A numpy array georeferenced like the input, with your own colours:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> mask = (forest.values == 2).astype("uint8")
>>> path = tf.write_raster(mask, "mask.tif", like=forest,
...                        colormap={0: (255, 255, 255), 1: (21, 128, 61)})
Floats with NaN: NaN is the NoData, or the value you choose:

>>> two = tf.write_raster(np.stack([mask, 1 - mask]), "stacks/two.tif", like=forest, band_names=["forest", "open"])
>>> tf.load_raster(two).band.values.tolist()
['forest', 'open']

terraflux.isochrone.name: isochrone
terraflux.isochrone.summary: Restoration Planner setup and isochrone maps (GuidosToolbox *Restoration Planner*).

doc.x:
- [`distance_to_resistance()`][terraflux.distance_to_resistance]: *Setup Tools -> Distance -> Resistance*, a
  resistance map growing with the distance to the foreground objects.
- [`isochrone_map()`][terraflux.isochrone_map]: *Assessment -> Isochrone Map A*, the accumulated cost
  (geodesic time) of reaching every pixel from object A across a resistance map.
- [`isochrone_map_ab()`][terraflux.isochrone_map_ab]: *Isochrone Map AB*, the cost of the cheapest route
  from A to B through every pixel, with the least-cost path.

The costs are those of GTB's ``ggeo`` program (miallib ``sqtgsym``): a step
between neighbouring pixels p and q (8-connectivity, diagonals included) costs
``(r[p] + r[q]) / 2``; foreground pixels (resistance 2) cost 1 and missing
pixels of the marker map block the way. The maps use GTB's display codes.

terraflux.isochrone.ISOCHRONE_CLASSES.name: ISOCHRONE_CLASSES
terraflux.isochrone.ISOCHRONE_CLASSES.value: {**{v: 'Cost, scaled to 0-100' for v in (0, 100)}, 101: 'Marker objects (A, B)', 102: 'Missing (marker value 3)', 103...

terraflux.isochrone.IsochroneResult.name: IsochroneResult
terraflux.isochrone.IsochroneResult.sig:
IsochroneResult(
    map: xr.DataArray | np.ndarray,
    cost: xr.DataArray | np.ndarray,
    lcp: xr.DataArray | np.ndarray | None,
    min_cost: int,
    max_cost: int,
)

i:
``uint8`` isochrone map in GTB's codes: 0-100 cost scaled between
``min_cost`` and ``max_cost``, 101 markers, 102 missing, 103 least-cost
path (AB), 104 unreachable.

Accumulated cost as GTB rounds it (``int64``; unreachable/missing: -2^31).
For map AB, the cost of the cheapest A-B route through each pixel.

Least-cost path mask (map AB), else ``None``: the pixels of minimal
A-B cost, thinned to a 1-pixel wide path as GTB's ``ggeo`` does.

terraflux.isochrone.distance_to_resistan.name: distance_to_resistance
terraflux.isochrone.distance_to_resistan.summary: Resistance growing with the distance to the foreground (GTB Setup Tools -> Distance -> Resistance).

doc.x:
``data`` is coded 0 missing, 1 background, 2 foreground. Background pixels
get ``round(distance + 2)`` capped at 100 (so 3 next to an object),
foreground 2 and missing 0. The distance is IDL's MORPH_DISTANCE as GTB
uses it (quasi-Euclidean; see [`influence_zones()`][terraflux.influence_zones] for the
remaining differences to IDL).

i: Threads (0 or ``None``: most of the cores).

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))   # 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest
>>> resistance = tf.distance_to_resistance(forest)
>>> int(resistance.min()), int(resistance.max())
(0, 38)

terraflux.isochrone.isochrone_map.name: isochrone_map
terraflux.isochrone.isochrone_map.summary: Accumulated cost from object A (GTB Restoration Planner -> Isochrone Map A).

i:
``uint8`` resistance map: 2 = foreground (cost 1), 3-100 = background
resistance (GTB's Restoration Planner coding; 0 costs nothing, as in GTB).

``uint8`` map of the same size: 0 background, 1 object A (a single
8-connected object), 3 missing (not crossed); 2 is ignored.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))   # 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest
>>> import numpy as np
>>> resistance = tf.distance_to_resistance(forest)
>>> objects = tf.accounting(forest)                     # the two largest forest objects
>>> ids = objects.ids.values
>>> marker = np.zeros(forest.shape, dtype="uint8")
>>> marker[ids == objects.largest[0][0]] = 1            # object A
>>> marker[ids == objects.largest[1][0]] = 2            # object B
>>> marker[forest.values == 0] = 3                      # missing: not crossed
>>> only_a = np.where(marker == 2, 0, marker).astype("uint8")
>>> rings = tf.isochrone_map(resistance, only_a)
>>> rings.min_cost, rings.max_cost
(2, 1166)

terraflux.isochrone.isochrone_map_ab.name: isochrone_map_ab

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))   # 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest
>>> import numpy as np
>>> resistance = tf.distance_to_resistance(forest)
>>> objects = tf.accounting(forest)                     # the two largest forest objects
>>> ids = objects.ids.values
>>> marker = np.zeros(forest.shape, dtype="uint8")
>>> marker[ids == objects.largest[0][0]] = 1            # object A
>>> marker[ids == objects.largest[1][0]] = 2            # object B
>>> marker[forest.values == 0] = 3                      # missing: not crossed
>>> route = tf.isochrone_map_ab(resistance, marker)
>>> route.min_cost, int(np.asarray(route.lcp).sum())
(210, 215)

Value treated as NA (default: the raster's nodata value).
Patch connectivity: 8 (queen's case, default) or 4 (rook's case).

cells from the patch edge).

``gyrate``: use the patch cell nearest to the centroid.

``relmutinf``): 4 or 8 neighbours, ordered pairs, and the logarithm

Band to read from multi-band files.

Out-of-core computation for rasters larger than memory: ``data`` must
be a file, read by blocks of this many rows (rounded up to a multiple
of 64; ``"auto"``: 64 rows, at least 32,768 cells). Small blocks are
worked on side by side, one per thread (about 64 rows per thread in
memory, at most 32 million cells); a larger block alone, on every
thread. Only those blocks and the patch tables stay in memory.
Results are identical to the in-memory ones; ``labels`` and
``to_raster`` give lazy rasters, computed and written block by block.
Threads of the C++ core (default: most of the cores).

``"landscapemetrics"`` (default) or ``"fragstats"``: with non-square
cells, left/right cell sides are as long as the cell height (the
physical perimeter; landscapemetrics takes the width); ``dcore_*``
summarise the sizes (ha) of the disjunct core areas instead of their
number per patch; ``shape`` is the raster SHAPE (perimeter over the
smallest perimeter of as many cells); ``_sd`` and ``_cv`` use the
standard deviation over n (landscapemetrics: R's ``sd()``, over n - 1);
the ``circle`` encloses the whole patch (landscapemetrics: the corners
of its first and last rows and columns only). Cells that are not
square keep ``shape`` and ``lsi`` as .25 perimeter / sqrt(area), as
pylandstats does.

``prox`` and ``simi`` (FRAGSTATS extras): patches within this
distance, in map units (NaN without it).
``connect``: patches of a class within this distance are connected.

Edge contrast weights (0-1) between classes for ``econ``, ``cwed`` and

``{(a, b): w}`` or ``{a: {b: w}}`` (symmetric; missing pairs give NaN),
and the weight of edges to NA and the map edge (default 0).

doc.x:
Each plot is cut from the raster as ``terra::crop(mask = TRUE)`` does
(grid window snapped to the nearest cell edges; every cell the plot
touches is kept, the others become NA) and its metrics are computed as
a landscape of its own. All plots are computed in parallel.

i:
A raster (see [`Landscape`][terraflux.Landscape]) or a list of rasters /
[`RasterCollection`][terraflux.RasterCollection] (``layer`` column).

Sample plots: an ``(n, 2)`` array of x/y coordinates or point
geometries (buffers of ``shape`` and ``size`` around them), or
polygons. Geometries can be shapely objects, a GeoSeries /
GeoDataFrame (anything with ``__geo_interface__``) or GeoJSON-like
dicts, in the raster's coordinates. As in landscapemetrics, the plot
area behind ``percentage_inside`` is geodesic when ``y`` has a CRS
(``y.crs``, e.g. a GeoDataFrame) and planar otherwise.

Buffer size around points: half the side of a square, or the radius
of a circle (landscapemetrics' 100-vertex polygon).

Add class-level rows (NA) for the classes of the whole raster that are
missing in a plot (with a row for class NA when the raster has NA
cells, as landscapemetrics does).
Warn when a plot lies less than 90 % inside the raster.
Also select the FRAGSTATS metrics missing in landscapemetrics.

Add the columns ``name``, ``type`` and ``function_name`` after
``value`` (landscapemetrics' ``sample_lsm(full_name = TRUE)`` drops
``function_name`` when ``return_raster = FALSE``, by a fixed column
index; it is kept here).

Add a column ``raster_sample_plots`` with each plot's raster (an
``xarray.DataArray``: the snapped window, NaN outside the plot and on
NA cells; ``None`` for a plot outside the raster).
Threads of the C++ core (default: most of the cores).

``level``, ``class``, ``id``, ``metric``, ``value``, ``plot_id`` and
``percentage_inside`` (area of the plot's cells over the plot area,
in %), ordered by plot, level, metric, class and id; plus ``layer``
for several rasters. A plot outside the raster (an error in
landscapemetrics) gives NA metrics and 0 %.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> landcover = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc"))
>>> import numpy as np
>>> xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax = tf.Landscape(landcover).extent
>>> points = np.array([[xmin + 5000, ymin + 5000], [xmax - 5000, ymax - 5000]])
>>> plots = tf.sample_metrics(landcover, points, size=1000, shape="circle",
...                           level="landscape", metric=["shdi", "np"])
>>> plots["plot_id"].unique().tolist()
[1, 2]

terraflux.lsm.tiled.name: tiled
terraflux.lsm.tiled.summary: Out-of-core landscapes: a raster file read by blocks of rows.

doc.x:
The file is read three times at most: once for its class values, once for
the patches and class adjacencies (enough for most metrics), and once more
for core areas, gyrate, circle and enn when those are asked for (plus once
for gyrate with ``cell_center``). Blocks are read ahead on a thread, and
blocks of few rows are prepared several at a time (each on some of the
threads) and merged in order, so the results do not depend on it; only those
blocks (with a few context rows) are in memory at a time, and the patch
tables. Maps of patch ids or metrics are lazy (dask): every block is read and
labelled again when it is computed.

i:

``sample_metrics``...). Patch-level metrics are correlated over patch
ids, class-level metrics over classes, landscape-level metrics over
layers (``layer`` column; needs several rasters). As in R's ``xtabs``,
values of the same id (class, layer) are summed, missing combinations
count as 0, NA values give NA correlations for their metric (whose
diagonal stays 1) and rows without id / class are left out.

triangle of the correlation matrix (column by column, as R).

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> landcover = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc"))
>>> table = tf.landscape_metrics(landcover, what=["lsm_p_area", "lsm_p_perim", "lsm_p_shape"])
>>> corr = tf.calculate_correlation(table, method="spearman")
>>> sorted(corr)
['patch']

doc.x:
Reimplements GuidosToolbox (GTB) Landscape Mosaic moving-window tool (Spatcon rule 7):
- [`landscape_mosaic()`][terraflux.landscape_mosaic]: Moving-window tri-polar land-cover mosaic classification
  (19 classes or 103 classes).
- [`landscape_mosaic_stats()`][terraflux.landscape_mosaic_stats]: 103-class frequency distribution and barycentric statistics.

Landscape Mosaic models the local composition of three land-cover components
within a moving observation window:
- Component 1: Agriculture / Non-forest / Matrix 1
- Component 2: Forest / Natural / Matrix 2
- Component 3: Developed / Antropic / Matrix 3
(and 0 = Missing / Unclassified).

The tri-polar percentages (p_agr, p_for, p_dev where p_agr + p_for + p_dev = 100%)
are mapped into discrete cells of a barycentric triangle (103 classes), which are
subsequently recoded into 19 ecologically meaningful landscape mosaic classes.

Riitters, K., Wickham, J., O'Neill, R., Jones, B., & Smith, E. (2000). Global-scale patterns
    of forest fragmentation. Conservation Ecology, 4(2), 3.
Vogt, P. & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis.
    European Journal of Remote Sensing, 50(1), 352-361.

terraflux.move.name: move
terraflux.move.summary: Movement ecology: animal tracks, their steps and their relation to the landscape.

doc.x:
Tracks are GeoDataFrames of points, one row per location, ordered by track and
time ([`load_tracks()`][terraflux.load_tracks] reads Movebank's files, `as_tracks()`
any table of locations). The first part is R's move2 (Kranstauber et al.
2024), the same numbers: the distance, speed, direction and turn of each step
(``sf`` / ``s2`` and ``lwgeom`` on the sphere and the ellipsoid), duplicates and
one location per interval, interpolation in time, tracks as lines, a local
projection, Brownian tracks. Computed in C++ with OpenMP.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    tracks = tf.load_tracks("study.csv")                    # Movebank's export
    tracks = tf.move.filter_unique(tracks)                  # one record per time and track
    tracks["speed"] = tf.move.speed(tracks)                 # m/s, NaN at the last location
    tracks["turn"] = tf.move.turn_angle(tracks, "deg")
    hourly = tf.move.filter_per_interval(tracks, "hour")
    lines = tf.move.track_lines(tracks)                     # one line per animal
    tf.write_vector(lines, "tracks.gpkg")

  drop those that only repeat another or hold less (each value equal to the
  other's or missing); a warning when some still remain;
* ``"subsets_equal"``: the same, with numbers equal within R's ``all.equal``
  tolerance (1.5e-8);

* ``"sample"``: one at random (R's ``sample.int`` after ``set.seed(seed)``, the

be duplicates (move2's ``additional_columns``). Returns a boolean mask.

doc.x:
Without ``times``, the records without a location (empty points) get one
between the locations before and after them. With ``times`` (datetimes, or
a unit such as ``"1 hour"`` or ``"15 mins"`` for a regular sequence from the
first to the last time), a record is added for each time within the span of
each track that the track does not have, and located. A location is placed
on the great circle between its neighbours in proportion to the time (in
longitude / latitude, and through it in a projected CRS, as move2 does with
s2), on the straight line without a CRS. Gaps longer than ``max_time_lag``
(seconds, or a ``pandas.Timedelta``) are left empty. ``omit``: keep only the
records at ``times``.

...                     "2024-01-01 03:20"], utc=True)

doc.x:
* ``"gamma"``: maximum likelihood by R's Nelder-Mead from the closed-form
  estimates (``fitdistrplus::fitdist``); steps of length 0 take the
  smallest other length. ``vcov``: of ``scale`` and ``shape``.
* ``"exp"``: the maximum likelihood rate, ``1 / mean(x)``. amt fits it by
  BFGS from that value, which fails for rates below 0.001 (mean steps over
  1000 m) and otherwise only adds the optimizer's noise.
* ``"lnorm"``: maximum likelihood by Nelder-Mead (``fitdistrplus``).
* ``"hnorm"``: ``sqrt(mean(x^2))``.
* ``"unif"``: the smallest and the largest value.
* ``"vonmises"``: ``kappa`` by maximum likelihood (``circular::mle.vonmises``),
  ``mu`` 0. ``vcov``: the variance of ``kappa`` (amt stores its standard
  error there).

terraflux.mspa_tiling.name: mspa_tiling
terraflux.mspa_tiling.summary: MSPA Tiling (GuidosToolbox *Image Analysis -> Pattern -> Morphological -> MSPA Tiling*).

doc.x:
GTB's way of running MSPA on maps too large for memory: the map is cut into
overlapping tiles (``tile_size`` pixels including an ``overlap``), MSPA runs
on every tile, and the tiles are put back together keeping, of each overlap,
the half nearest to each tile. As GTB warns, this is an approximation: MSPA
classes depend on whole objects (e.g. loops, bridges, islets, openings), so
near the seams they can differ from MSPA of the whole map when objects are
larger than the overlap. [`mspa_tiled()`][terraflux.mspa_tiled] reproduces GTB's tiling exactly,
including its shortcuts for tiles without background or without foreground.

With a raster path the map is processed out of core: every tile is read from
and written to disk by window, so memory holds only the tiles in progress.

terraflux.nlm.name: nlm
terraflux.nlm.summary: Neutral landscape models: simulated landscapes that serve as null models.

doc.x:
A port of the R package NLMR (Sciaini et al. 2018): with the same seed each
model gives the same landscape as NLMR, bit for bit (R's random number
generator and the C++ library NLMR is built with are reproduced), computed in
C++ with OpenMP.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    r = tf.nlm.random(100, 100, seed=42)           # xarray.DataArray, 0-1
    classes = tf.nlm.classify(r, weighting=[0.6, 0.4])
    tf.landscape_metrics(classes, ["pland", "np"], level="class")

distance_gradient(

    n_threads: int | None = None,

doc.x: The distance of every cell to a rectangular origin.

i:
The origin rectangle, 1-based and inclusive. With ``nlmr_compat=True``
as NLMR applies it: ``(first row, last row, first column, last column)``
(NLMR documents ``xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax`` but indexes the raster as
``[rows, columns]``); otherwise ``(first column, last column, first row,
last row)``.

Reproduce NLMR exactly: ``terra::distance`` treats a raster of at most
360 x 90 cells as longitude/latitude (terra's default CRS for such an
extent) and returns great-circle distances in metres (haversine on a

terraflux.nlm._classify.classify.summary: Classify a continuous landscape into categories (NLMR's ``landscape_classify``).

doc.x:
Three ways, as NLMR:

- ``weighting``: class proportions (cumulative, relative to their sum; ``None``
  entries share what is left of 1); the class boundaries are the values at
  those proportions of the sorted cells, the first class starting at 0 (values
  below 0 are left out);
- ``real_land``: the proportions of the classes of a real landscape (after
  removing ``mask_val``, whose cells are also removed from ``x``);
- ``n``: Jenks natural breaks into ``n`` classes (at most the number of unique
  values). Jenks' algorithm costs O(n_classes x cells^2): keep it to small maps.

``weighting`` wins over ``n`` when both are given.

(the DataArray's nodata value).

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> r = tf.nlm.random(20, 20, seed=3)
>>> c = tf.nlm.classify(r, weighting=[0.5, 0.25, 0.25])
>>> [int((c == k).sum()) for k in (1, 2, 3)]

>>> c.shape
(384, 384)

terraflux.nlm._spectral.fbm.summary: Fractional Brownian motion neutral landscape model (NLMR's ``nlm_fbm``).

doc.x:
A fractal surface from a power-law spectrum ``|k|^-(fract_dim + 1)`` with
random phases (inverse FFT), centred and scaled to unit standard deviation
of the steps between neighbouring cells. ``fract_dim`` is the Hurst-like
exponent alpha of NLMR (0 < alpha <= 2): small values give rough surfaces,
large ones smooth ones; alpha = 2 is a random plane.

NLMR 1.4 disabled ``nlm_fbm`` when RandomFields left CRAN and ships this
method as its internal ``simulate_fbm``; the results here are that
function's, rescaled as NLMR's previous ``nlm_fbm`` did.

i:
Seed of R's generator: the same seed gives NLMR's surface. ``None`` draws
one, stored in ``attrs["seed"]``.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> f = tf.nlm.fbm(64, 64, fract_dim=1.5, seed=2)
>>> f.shape, float(f.max())
((64, 64), 1.0)

doc.x:
A stationary Gaussian field with an exponential covariance
``mag_var * exp(-d / autocorr_range)``, simulated exactly by circulant
embedding (FFT on a grid twice as large in each direction), plus a nugget
(white noise of variance ``nug``) and a mean.

NLMR 1.4 disabled ``nlm_gaussianfield`` when RandomFields left CRAN and ships
this method as its internal ``simulate_gaussian_field``; the results here are
that function's, rescaled as NLMR's previous ``nlm_gaussianfield`` did.

i: Range of the spatial autocorrelation, in cells.
Variance of the nugget (uncorrelated noise); 0 for none.

Seed of R's generator: the same seed gives NLMR's field. ``None`` draws
one, stored in ``attrs["seed"]``.

Standard deviation of the displacement at the first step.

terraflux.parallel.name: parallel
terraflux.parallel.summary: Many independent tasks on this computer and on other computers of the local network.

doc.x:
A computer lends itself to the group with ``terraflux-py worker`` (the first time
``terraflux-py worker --join <code>``, with the code that ``terraflux-py helpers invite``
shows on the computer that will use it). Functions that run many independent tasks take
``on=tf.helpers()`` and run them here and on the helpers, with the same results as on
this computer alone::

    import terraflux as tf

    with tf.helpers() as pool:
        runs = tf.batch("fad", "tiles/", "fad_out/", on=pool)
        ens = tf.simulate.scenarios(model, start, drivers, replicates=200, seed=1, on=pool)

Helpers only run terraflux's own operations, never code sent to them: a task is the
name of an operation, its parameters and its input files. They connect out to the
computer that coordinates (only that one needs a firewall rule), authenticated by the
group's secret, over TLS.

tool runs on it and its result over the tile proper goes into place: the same
values as on the whole raster, for tools that see only a neighbourhood (moving
windows, lines of sight, slopes). A raster read lazily (``tf.load_raster(path,

``"window_metrics"``, ``"surface.geomorphons"``, ``"surface.tri"``,
``"surface.terrain"``, ``"surface.curvature"``, ``"surface.trasp"``,
``"surface.dissection"`` and ``"services.carbon"``, whose tiles give the same bits
as the whole map; required for other tools. The window means of
``"surface.tpi"``, ``"vrm"``, ``"srr"``, ``"hsp"`` and ``"spherical_sd"`` are
running sums along the rows, so their tiles agree to about 1e-12).

Save the result there (``tf.save``) and return its path.

result class when every part of it is a map (else a dict of its maps).

i:

terraflux.prioritize.name: prioritize
terraflux.prioritize.summary: Spatial conservation prioritization: ranking the cells of a landscape, or selecting the best set of planning units by optimization.

doc.x:
A port of Zonation 5 (Lehtinen, Moilanen et al., University of Helsinki; GPL-3):
the cells are ranked from the least to the most important for a set of
features (species, habitats, ecosystem services), weighted, with costs,
hierarchical masks and the core-area (CAZ) or additive-benefit (ABF) marginal
loss rules; with performance curves of how much of every feature the best
fractions of the landscape keep. Same results as the z5 program, bit for bit,
computed in C++ with OpenMP.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    res = tf.prioritize.zonation(["sp1.tif", "sp2.tif", "sp3.tif"], weights=[2, 1, 1])
    res.rank                      # 0 = lowest priority, ~1 = highest
    res.feature_curves            # fraction of every feature kept
    res.write("zonation_output")  # Zonation's files

    # or an existing Zonation 5 project, with z5's switches
    res = tf.prioritize.run_project("settings.z5", "-w -X", mode="CAZ2")

The optimization paradigm of prioritizr (Hanson et al.; GPL-3): a problem of
planning units, features, an objective, targets and constraints, compiled to
the same mixed-integer model as prioritizr and solved on HiGHS (built in) or
Gurobi::

    p = (tf.prioritize.problem(cost, features)
           .add_min_set_objective()
           .add_relative_targets(0.3)
           .add_binary_decisions())
    sol = p.solve()
    sol.selection                 # 1 = selected
    sol.coverage                  # targets met per feature

With management zones (prioritizr's zones), every planning unit goes to at
most one zone, each with its own cost and its own contribution to the
features::

    p = (tf.prioritize.problem({"protect": c1, "use": c2}, features,
                               contribution={"use": 0.5})
           .add_min_set_objective()
           .add_relative_targets(0.3)                   # summed over the zones
           .add_relative_targets(0.1, zone="protect"))  # and 10% in protection
    sol = p.solve()
    sol.zones                     # the zone of every unit

terraflux.prioritize._examples.example_d.name: example_data
terraflux.prioritize._examples.example_d.summary: Path of an example data set for prioritization: **Serra Verde**, an imaginary coastal region of 60 x 90 cells of 1 km (SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 23S). Mountains rise in the north-west; the coastal plain has three cities, a highway and two rivers; the ocean in the south-east has no data, which leaves 4825 planning units on land. The data are synthetic, made to behave like real planning data.

i:
``"cost"``: land cost (thousand USD per km²), cheap in the mountains, dear near cities and roads;
``"features"``: habitat suitability (0-1) of eight features, a stack with the bands
``jaguar`` (widespread), ``lowland_tapir`` (river valleys), ``harpy_eagle`` (remote mountain
forest), ``maned_wolf`` (western grasslands), ``golden_lion_tamarin`` (two small lowland
fragments: rare), ``neotropical_otter`` (the rivers), ``araucaria_forest`` (cold highlands) and
``mangrove`` (a thin coastal strip: rare);
``"protected"``: three existing protected areas (1); ``"urban"``: the cities (1);
``"condition"``: habitat condition (0 degraded, 1 pristine); ``"regions"``: three
administrative regions (1-3); ``"carbon"``: carbon stock (t/ha); ``"terminals"``: the two
mountain parks to link by a corridor (1); ``"threats"``: ``deforestation`` and ``fire``
intensity (0-1); ``"elevation"``: relative elevation (0-1); ``"lines"``: the ``rivers`` and the
``roads`` (1), for maps.

For restoration plans (`restoration_problem()`): ``"land_cover"``: the share (0-1) of six
classes in every cell, the bands ``forest``, ``savanna``, ``mangrove`` (natural), ``pasture``,
``cropland`` (anthropic) and ``urban``; ``"past_cover"``: the share of the three natural classes
in the past, before most of the conversion; ``"footprint"``: the human footprint index (0-50);
``"ecoregions"``: four ecoregions (1 coast, 2 lowland forest, 3 montane forest, 4 savanna);
``"carbon_potential"``: the carbon restored vegetation would hold after 30 years (t/ha).

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> features = tf.load_raster(tf.prioritize.example_data("features"))
>>> features.shape
(8, 60, 90)
>>> [str(b) for b in features.band.values][:3]

doc.x:
With zones: ``edge_factor`` one or one per zone, and ``zones`` how much the boundary between
two zones counts: ``"same"`` (the default, prioritizr's identity matrix: the boundary of every
zone's units), ``"any"``, or a symmetric zones x zones matrix (values from -1 to 1; the diagonal
for units of the same zone, the other cells for neighbours in different zones; a DataFrame by

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_c.summary: Reward selecting connected units: ``penalty`` x the connectivity of every pair selected together (a symmetric matrix of every unit; the diagonal rewards a unit alone). With zones, ``zones`` as in [`add_boundary_penalties()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_boundary_penalties] (how much a connection between two zones counts).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_c.name: add_contiguity_constraints
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_c.summary: The selected units must form one contiguous patch. ``data``: an adjacency matrix of every unit; by default units that share an edge (raster cells, 4 directions) or that touch (polygons).

doc.x:
The model is exact: a spanning arborescence of the selected units, with a flow that rules out
cycles. prioritizr's formulation (a tree whose edges always run from a unit to one of a lower
index) is a restriction: it misses patches in which a unit has no selected neighbour of a higher
index, so it can return a costlier patch than the best, or call a feasible problem infeasible.
On HiGHS a minimum set is solved by a patch heuristic (patches grown from every unit, pruned, then
perturbed and regrown), a first patch from that restriction, directed cuts at the root, then the
exact MIP from the best patch, with the cuts separated at its nodes too. Contiguity stays the
hardest spatial rule: give it a time limit on more than a few hundred units (the heuristic and the
cuts take their shares of it).

With zones, ``zones`` is a binary symmetric zones x zones matrix: the zones linked through it
form a cluster whose units (in any of its zones) must form one patch; a zone with 0 on the
diagonal is free. By default (``"same"``) the units of every zone form one patch.

or one value per planning unit; NaN leaves a unit alone.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_manual_targets
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Targets from a table, one row per target: ``feature`` (name), ``type`` (``"relative"`` or ``"absolute"``), ``target`` and, optionally, ``sense`` (``">="``, the default, ``"<="`` or ``"="``). A feature may have several targets, or none. With zones, an optional ``zone`` column: a zone or a list of zones whose amounts the target adds up (default: every zone; a relative target as in [`add_relative_targets()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_relative_targets]).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_cover_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Maximum cover: within the budget, the most features held at all (any amount above zero, weighted); no targets.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_features_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Maximum features: within the budget, the most targets met (weighted).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_n_targets_met_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: [`add_max_features_objective()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_max_features_objective] under prioritizr 9's name (the model is 8.0.6's, with the small cost term that breaks ties, which prioritizr 9 dropped).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_phylo_div_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Maximum phylogenetic diversity: within the budget, the most total length of the branches of a phylogeny with a target met below them (Faith 1992). ``tree``: an ``tf.bio`` tree ([`read_tree()`][terraflux.bio.read_tree]) or a Newick string, whose tips are the features.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_phylo_end_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Maximum phylogenetic endemism: as [`add_max_phylo_div_objective()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_max_phylo_div_objective], every branch's length divided by the total amount of the features below it (Rosauer et al. 2009).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_utility_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Maximum utility: within the budget, the most of the features' amounts (weighted); no targets.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_max_wtd_sum_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: [`add_max_utility_objective()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_max_utility_objective] under prioritizr 9's name (the model is 8.0.6's, with the small cost term that breaks ties, which prioritizr 9 dropped).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_min_extinction_risk_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.sig: add_min_extinction_risk_objective(budget: float, z=0.25, segments: int = 16) -> Problem
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Minimum extinction risk (our extension): within the budget, the least sum over the features (weighted) of the risk the species-area relationship gives, 1 - (held / total)^z (Pereira & Daily 2006; z = 0.25 by default, one value or one per feature), as a piecewise-linear function through ``segments`` + 1 points of the curve (exact at them, slightly above in between). No targets.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_min_largest_shortfall_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Minimum largest shortfall: within the budget, the least of the largest shortfall of any target, as a share of the target.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_min_penalties_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Minimum penalties: meet the targets within the budget with the least penalties (the penalties come in a later phase: until then any solution that meets them is optimal).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_min_set_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Minimum set: meet every target at the least cost.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.name: add_min_shortfall_objective
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_m.summary: Minimum shortfall: within the budget, the least sum of the targets' shortfalls, each as a share of its target (weighted by [`add_feature_weights()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_feature_weights]).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.name: add_neighbor_constraints
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.sig: add_neighbor_constraints(k: int, clamp: bool = True, data=None, zones=None) -> Problem
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.summary: [`add_neighbors_constraints()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_neighbors_constraints] under the name of prioritizr's newer versions.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.name: add_neighbor_penalties
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.summary: Reward selecting neighbouring units together, against fragmentation (prioritizr 9's ``add_neighbor_penalties``, after Önal and Briers 2002): ``penalty`` for every pair of selected neighbours. These are the connectivity penalties ([`add_connectivity_penalties()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_connectivity_penalties]) of a binary symmetric adjacency matrix: ``data``, a matrix of every unit, by default units that share an edge (raster cells, 4 directions) or that touch (polygons). With zones, ``zones`` as in [`add_boundary_penalties()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_boundary_penalties] (how much neighbours in two zones count; default ``"same"``).

doc.x:
On minimum sets they keep the cut engine's form (pair rewards), like the boundary penalties,
and lighter models than contiguity constraints: a way to cluster large problems.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.name: add_neighbors_constraints
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.sig: add_neighbors_constraints(k: int, clamp: bool = True, data=None, zones=None) -> Problem
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_n.summary: Every selected unit must have at least ``k`` selected neighbours (``clamp``: at most as many as it has). ``data``: an adjacency matrix of every unit, by default as [`add_contiguity_constraints()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_contiguity_constraints]. With zones, ``k`` one or one per zone, and ``zones`` a binary zones x zones matrix of the zones whose units count as neighbours of a unit in a zone (default ``"same"``: only its own zone's).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_p.name: add_proportion_decisions
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_p.summary: Any share (0-1) of every planning unit can be selected (a linear program).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_r.name: add_relative_targets
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_r.summary: Targets as shares (0-1) of every feature's total amount (one value or one per feature).

doc.x:
With zones, the targets are met by the sum over the zones of the features' amounts in them,
each counted by its zone's contribution: a share of the feature's total (the base features
of the contributions; with every zone's own features, the sum of its totals in the zones, as
prioritizr). ``zone``: targets of one zone (shares of the feature's total in that zone) or of a
list of zones, added to the others (targets of the same zones replace the earlier ones). A
matrix (features x zones) gives every zone its own targets (prioritizr's form).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.name: add_semicontinuous_decisions
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.summary: Any share of every planning unit up to ``upper_limit`` can be selected.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.name: add_shuffle_portfolio
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.sig:
add_shuffle_portfolio(
    number_solutions: int = 10,
    remove_duplicates: bool = True,
    seed: int | None = None,
) -> Problem
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.summary: ``number_solutions`` solves of the model with its planning units (and other columns) in random orders: different solutions of equal quality when there are ties (``remove_duplicates``: keep distinct ones).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.name: add_subregional_targets
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_s.summary: Targets within sub-regions (an extension: prioritizr has none), added to the other targets: one row per target, ``region``, ``feature`` (name), ``target``, optionally ``type`` (``"relative"``, the default, or ``"absolute"``) and ``sense`` (``">="``, ``"<="``, ``"="``). A relative target is a share of the feature's total in the region, over every unit with or without a cost, as the other relative targets are. With zones, an optional ``zone`` column (a zone or a list of zones, default every zone), as in [`add_relative_targets()`][terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.add_relative_targets].

i:
The region of every unit: with raster units, a raster on their grid (NaN: no region);
with tables and polygons, a column name or one value per row (missing: no region).
The targets (a DataFrame or a dict of columns).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.compi.name: compile
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.compi.summary: The model prioritizr's ``compile()`` gives for this problem.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.solve.name: solve
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.solve.summary: Solve the problem on its solver (HiGHS unless another was added): a [`Solution`][terraflux.prioritize.Solution].

i:
A solution to start from: one value per planning unit, or a
Zonation ranking to build one from: ``"zonation"`` (Zonation's
CAZ2 on the problem's features, with the cost raster if the units
are cells), a [`ZonationResult`][terraflux.prioritize.ZonationResult] or a
rank raster. The units go in from the highest rank down until
every target is met (locked-in units always, locked-out never);
the solver then drops those not needed and goes on from there.

terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.zones.name: zones
terraflux.prioritize._milp.Problem.zones.summary: The names of the management zones (empty without zones).

terraflux.prioritize._milp.h3_units.name: h3_units
terraflux.prioritize._milp.h3_units.sig: h3_units(cost: xr.DataArray, resolution: int, n_threads: int | None = None)
terraflux.prioritize._milp.h3_units.summary: H3 hexagons as planning units: the hexagons of an H3 ``resolution`` that cover a cost raster, with their cost.

doc.x:
Pass them to `problem()` as polygons (``cost_column="cost"``): the
features' amounts are then summed over every hexagon like any polygon's.

i:
The cost raster (with a CRS). Every hexagon that covers a cell with a
cost is a planning unit; its cost is the sum of the costs of the cells
it covers, each weighted by the exact share of the cell inside it.
The H3 resolution (0-15; 7 is about 5 km², 8 about 0.7 km²).
Threads for the sums (default: most of the cores).

One hexagon per row (in the raster's CRS, its six vertices
reprojected): ``h3`` (the cell's index) and ``cost``.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> hexes = tf.prioritize.h3_units(cost, 8)
>>> p = tf.prioritize.problem(hexes, features, cost_column="cost")

terraflux.prioritize._milp.problem.name: problem
terraflux.prioritize._milp.problem.sig:
problem(
    x,
    features=None,
    *,
    cost_column=None,
    rij=None,
    contribution=None,
    zones=None,
) -> Problem

i:
The planning units and their cost: a raster (the cells with a cost are
the planning units), polygons (a GeoDataFrame) or a table, both with a
``cost_column`` (the rows with a cost are the planning units).

With a raster: the features' rasters on the same grid (a ``(band, y,
x)`` DataArray, a Dataset or a list of rasters). With polygons: the
features' rasters, summed over every polygon weighted by the exact
share of every cell it covers (as exactextractr, which prioritizr
uses). With a table: the names of its feature columns, or, with
``rij``, a table of the features (``id``, ``name``).
The cost column of a table.

Marxan-style amounts (``pu``, ``species``, ``amount``) with a table of
planning units that has an ``id`` column (with zones, a ``zone``
column too).

Management zones: every planning unit goes to at most one zone, each
with its own cost (``x``: a mapping zone -> cost raster, a raster with
a band per zone, or ``cost_column`` a mapping zone -> column). The
features are given once, and ``contribution`` says how much of them
counts in each zone: a mapping zone -> a number, one number per
feature, or a raster (a column with tables) of factors per unit
(zones not listed count fully). Instead, ``features`` may be a
mapping zone -> that zone's own features (prioritizr's ``zones()``).

With ``rij`` and a ``zone`` column: the zones table (``id``,
``name``), in the order of the cost columns.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(tf.prioritize.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(tf.prioritize.example_data("features"))
>>> p = (tf.prioritize.problem(cost, features)
...        .add_min_set_objective()
...        .add_relative_targets(0.3)
...        .add_binary_decisions())
>>> sol = p.solve()
>>> sol.status
'optimal'
>>> bool(sol.coverage["met"].all())
True

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.Tra.name: TradeOffs
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.Tra.sig: TradeOffs(table: pd.DataFrame = ..., solutions: list = ..., criterion: str = '')
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.Tra.summary: Candidate solutions over a trade-off parameter.

i:
One row per candidate: ``value`` (the penalty, the cost threshold or the budget), ``cost``, the
criterion traded off against it (``boundary``, ``connectivity``, ``shortfall``...), the
objective, status and gap; ``topsis`` and ``knee`` mark the candidates those methods choose.
The candidates' [`Solution`][terraflux.prioritize.Solution]\ s, in the table's order.

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.Tra.name: best
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.Tra.summary: The candidate the method chooses (``"topsis"`` with equal weights, or ``"knee"``).

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.name: calibrate
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.sig:
calibrate(
    make,
    values,
    criterion,
    name: str = 'criterion',
    n_threads: int | None = None,
    on=None,
) -> TradeOffs
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.summary: Any trade-off parameter: ``make(value)`` gives the problem for every value (a feature's weight, a target, a penalty of any kind...), ``criterion(problem, solution)`` the quantity traded off against the cost (smaller is better). The candidates' table as `calibrate_penalty()`'s (TOPSIS, knee), solved in parallel. ``on=tf.helpers()`` solves them on the helpers of this computer's group too ([`parallel`][terraflux.parallel]).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> def make(w):
...     return P.problem(cost, features).add_max_utility_objective(5000).add_feature_weights([w, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1])
>>> def lost(q, s):
...     rep = P.eval_feature_representation_summary(q, s)
...     return 1 - rep["relative_held"].iloc[1]
>>> cal = P.calibrate(make, [1, 10], lost, name="tapir_lost")
>>> list(cal.table.columns[:3])
['value', 'cost', 'tapir_lost']

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.name: calibrate_budget
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.sig:
calibrate_budget(
    p,
    penalty: str = 'boundary',
    thresholds=None,
    inflation=None,
    data=None,
    edge_factor: float = 0.5,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
    on=None,
) -> TradeOffs
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.summary: The hierarchical approach: the least cost solution first (``p``, a min set problem without the penalty, solved to optimality), then the least penalty within cost thresholds above its cost (``thresholds``, or the cost x (1 + ``inflation``); default inflation 1e-5 to 4 in 9 steps, the thresholds rounded up as in prioritizr's tutorial). Solves in parallel.

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> c, f = P.coarsen(cost, features, 6)
>>> p = P.problem(c, f).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> cal = P.calibrate_budget(p.add_highs_solver(gap=0.05), "boundary", inflation=[0.1, 0.5, 1.0])
>>> len(cal.table)
3
>>> bool((cal.table["cost"] <= cal.table["value"] + 1e-6).all())
True

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.name: calibrate_penalty
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.sig:
calibrate_penalty(
    p,
    penalty: str = 'boundary',
    values=None,
    n: int = 9,
    data=None,
    edge_factor: float = 0.5,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
    on=None,
) -> TradeOffs
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.cal.summary: The blended approach: the problem solved with a range of penalty weights (``values``; default ``n`` values evenly spaced in log scale over 1/100 to 100 times the Cohon et al. penalty), every candidate's cost and criterion (boundary length, connectivity, ...), and the candidates TOPSIS and the knee of the curve choose. ``p``: the problem without the penalty. Solves in parallel. ``on=tf.helpers()`` solves them on the helpers of this computer's group too ([`parallel`][terraflux.parallel]).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> c, f = P.coarsen(cost, features, 6)
>>> p = P.problem(c, f).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> cal = P.calibrate_penalty(p.add_highs_solver(gap=0.05), "boundary", values=[0.001, 0.01, 0.1])
>>> cal.table[["value", "status"]]
   value   status
0  0.001  optimal
1  0.010  optimal
2  0.100  optimal
>>> best = cal.best("topsis")

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.coh.name: cohon_penalty
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.coh.sig:
cohon_penalty(
    p,
    penalty: str = 'boundary',
    data=None,
    edge_factor: float = 0.5,
    gap: float = 0.0,
)
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.coh.summary: The penalty of Cohon et al. (1979): the trade-off rate between the solution with the least cost (``p`` as given, a min set problem without the penalty) and the one with the least penalty (min penalties within a budget above every unit's cost): |cost difference / criterion difference|, rounded to 5 decimals. Returns (penalty, a table of the two ideal solutions' cost and criterion).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> c, f = P.coarsen(cost, features, 6)
>>> p = P.problem(c, f).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> value, ideals = P.cohon_penalty(p.add_highs_solver(gap=0.05))
>>> value > 0
True
>>> list(ideals.columns)
['solution', 'cost', 'boundary']

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.ite.name: iterative_solve
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.ite.sig: iterative_solve(p, update, steps: int, lock_previous: bool = False)
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.ite.summary: Solve, change the problem, solve again: ``update(step, solution, problem)`` gives the next problem (for instance from the landscape a ``tf.simulate`` step leaves, with the solution's cells protected by `protected_cells()` in the simulation's rules), or ``None`` to stop. With ``lock_previous``, every solution's units stay selected in the next problem (protected areas that accumulate). Returns the solutions and a table (step, cost, units, status).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> p = P.problem(cost, features).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> def update(step, sol, q):
...     return q.add_relative_targets(0.2 + 0.05 * (step + 1))
>>> sols, table = P.iterative_solve(p, update, 3, lock_previous=True)
>>> table["step"].tolist()
[0, 1, 2]
>>> bool(table["cost"].is_monotonic_increasing)
True

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.kne.name: knee_point
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.kne.summary: The knee (elbow) of a trade-off curve: the point farthest from the straight line between its ends, both axes scaled to 0-1 (the points in the order of x). Returns its position.

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.mea.name: mean_sd
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.mea.summary: plangea's choice of weights (``post_choose_weights``): every criterion (a column of ``decision``) rescaled to 0-1 over the alternatives (a constant one to 1), the "-" ones (smaller is better) inverted, and every alternative scored by the mean of its criteria divided by their standard deviation (good on all of them at once). Returns ``mean``, ``sd``, ``score`` (larger is better) and ``rank`` (1 = best). plangea took the mean after adding the deviation as a column (the mean of the criteria and the deviation); here it is the criteria's.

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> tf.prioritize.mean_sd([[1.0, 9.0], [4.0, 6.0], [9.0, 1.0]], impacts=["+", "+"])["rank"].tolist()
[2.5, 1.0, 2.5]

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.par.name: pareto_front
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.par.sig:
pareto_front(
    p,
    budgets=None,
    n: int = 10,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
    on=None,
) -> TradeOffs
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.par.summary: The trade-off between cost and representation: the least total shortfall of the targets (min shortfall objective: the sum of the shortfalls as shares of their targets) within ``n`` budgets evenly spaced up to the least-cost solution's cost (above the cost of the locked-in units, which every budget includes), or the ``budgets`` given. ``p``: a problem with targets (its objective is replaced). The table adds ``met`` (targets met) and ``efficient`` (no other candidate is cheaper and not worse, or better and not dearer).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> p = P.problem(cost, features).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> front = P.pareto_front(p, n=4)
>>> front.table[["met", "efficient"]]
   met  efficient
0    1       True
1    3       True
2    2       True
3    8       True

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.pro.name: protected_cells
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.pro.summary: The selected cells of a raster solution as a boolean raster (for ``tf.simulate``'s restrictions).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> p = P.problem(cost, features).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> sol = p.solve()
>>> mask = P.protected_cells(sol)
>>> mask.dtype.name
'bool'

terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.top.name: topsis
terraflux.prioritize._milp_calibrate.top.summary: TOPSIS (as R's ``topsis`` package): the alternatives (rows of ``decision``) scored by their closeness to the ideal (``impacts``: "+" larger is better, "-" smaller is better, per column; equal ``weights`` by default). Returns ``score`` (0-1, larger is better) and ``rank`` (1 = best).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> tf.prioritize.topsis([[1.0, 9.0], [4.0, 4.0], [9.0, 1.0]], impacts=["-", "-"])["rank"].tolist()
[2.5, 1.0, 2.5]

terraflux.prioritize._milp_eval.eval_asy.name: eval_asym_connectivity_summary
terraflux.prioritize._milp_eval.eval_asy.summary: As `eval_connectivity_summary()` for an asymmetric matrix (its diagonal counted once).

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> P = tf.prioritize
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(P.example_data("features"))
>>> p = P.problem(cost, features).add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.2).add_binary_decisions()
>>> sol = p.solve()
>>> import scipy.sparse as sp
>>> cm = P.connectivity_matrix(cost, features[0])
>>> asym = sp.triu(cm).tocsr()
>>> round(P.eval_asym_connectivity_summary(p, sol, asym)["asym_connectivity"].item(), 2)

terraflux.prioritize._milp_eval.eval_bou.name: eval_boundary_summary

cell's natural land keeps the habitat that would be lost (its ``loss`` times the threat);
converting it takes that habitat away. The benefit is the sum over the species of the risk
without the plan minus the risk with it (negative when conversion raises the risk).

doc.x:
``form="linear"``: linearised at the plan of nothing ([`intactness_gradient()`][terraflux.intactness_gradient];
with ``method="steps"`` it is recomputed at every step, as plangea does). ``form="exact"``: the
total intactness itself, which is not concave (a sum of exponentials of the footprint): the exact
method improves the plan by successive concave minorants (the tangent of every pair's
exponential, which never overestimates; each step solved exactly, the benefit never falls) to a
local optimum, and bounds the best plan by the secant of every pair over the footprints the
plans can reach. The status is ``"optimal"`` when the two meet within the tolerance, else

terraflux.prioritize._restoration.Restor.name: solve
terraflux.prioritize._restoration.Restor.sig: solve(method: str = 'exact', steps: int = 1) -> RestorationSolution
terraflux.prioritize._restoration.Restor.summary: Solve the problem.

doc.x:
``method="exact"``: the optimum within the solver's ``tolerance`` (relative, between the plan's
benefit and a bound on the best one). Simplicial decomposition: every vertex of the set of plans
is the solution of a linear program over the units with the gradient of the benefits as its
objective and only the targets and the budget as rows; the plan is the best mix of the vertices
found (a small concave problem, by SLSQP); the bound is F(x) + grad F(x) . (v - x), v the
next vertex (valid because the benefits are concave). The minimum cost: a bisection on the
budget, each step the most benefit for it; the bound is the largest budget proven too small.

``method="steps"``: plangea's procedure, for comparison: every cell scored by its weighted
benefits (each layer scaled by 1 / 10^trunc(log10(max))) per cost, the area targets met in
``steps`` equal parts, the extinction-risk and intactness layers recomputed after every part.
It is a heuristic: its benefit is at most the exact one, and depends on ``steps``. Area
targets only (no budget, no minimum cost).

A cell counts in a level when its share is above it (the gradient).

eval_risk_reduction(
    problem: RestorationProblem,
    solution,
    z_sd: float | None = None,
    *,
    benefit: str | None = None,
    method: str = 'correlated',
    step: float = 1e-06,

terraflux.prioritize._restoration.eval_r.summary: The reduction of the extinction risk a plan brings (plangea's ``multi_exrisk_aggregate``), with the uncertainty of the species-area exponent z.

i: A `RestorationSolution`, or the share restored per unit (or a raster).

The standard deviation of z (plangea: 0.1): a number for every species, one per species (in
the order of the benefit's species) or a mapping species -> deviation (0 for the others); None:
no uncertainty.
The extinction-risk benefit to evaluate (default: the first).

How the species' sensitivities to z add up. ``"correlated"`` (the default): the species' z err
together (one z for all of them, or per-species values from one source), so the total's
deviation is |sum_s d reduction_s / dz_s sd_s| (the delta method on the total).
``"independent"`` sums them in quadrature and ``"linear"`` sums their absolute values, plangea's
two forms (they treat the species' z as separate parameters).

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import xarray as xr
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> cover = xr.DataArray(np.array([[[0.6, 0.0, 0.3]], [[0.2, 0.1, 0.0]], [[0.2, 0.9, 0.7]]]),
...                      dims=("band", "y", "x"), coords={"band": ["forest", "savanna", "crops"]})
>>> ranges = xr.DataArray(np.ones((2, 1, 3)), dims=("band", "y", "x"), coords={"band": ["toucan", "rhea"]})
>>> veg = tf.original_vegetation(cover, ["forest", "savanna"], ["crops"])
>>> aoh = tf.sdm.area_of_habitat(ranges, cover, ["forest", "savanna"], original=veg, cell_area=1.0,
...                              suitability={"toucan": ["forest"], "rhea": ["savanna"]})
>>> p = (tf.prioritize.restoration_problem(veg, cell_area=1.0)
...        .add_extinction_risk_benefit(aoh).add_area_target(0.8))
>>> sol = p.solve()
>>> rr = tf.prioritize.eval_risk_reduction(p, sol, z_sd=0.1)
>>> round(rr.total, 4), round(rr.sd, 4)
(0.269, 0.0871)

terraflux.prioritize._restoration.restor.summary: A restoration problem: how much of every converted cell to restore (and of natural land to conserve or convert).

doc.x:
The planning units are the cells with land an action can take; the decision is the share x_i of
each, from 0 to the share that can be times ``limit``. Then add benefits
(`add_extinction_risk_benefit()`,
`add_linear_benefit()`, `add_intactness_benefit()`),
targets (`add_area_target()`), a budget, and solve.

i:
The share of every cell that can be restored: a raster, or a
[`OriginalVegetation`][terraflux.OriginalVegetation] (its anthropic share).

The share of every cell's natural land that conservation can keep (plangea's ``C``): without
the plan, ``threat`` of it is lost (plangea: all of it). The benefits count what conserving
saves.

The share of every cell's natural land that can be converted (plangea's ``D``, a demand for
land met where it costs the least benefit). With ``restorable`` too, the plan restores some
cells and converts others (plangea's ``R + D``). Not with ``conservable``.

plangea's bound limit: a number or a raster multiplying the shares, or a mapping action ->
limit.

The share of the conservable land lost without conservation, in [0, 1]: a number or a raster
(default 1, plangea's).

The cells' area in km²: a number, a raster, or None (from the grid, see
[`cell_area_km2()`][terraflux.sdm.cell_area_km2]).

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> anthropic = rng.random((20, 30)) * 0.6
>>> carbon = rng.random((20, 30)) * 100
>>> p = (tf.prioritize.restoration_problem(anthropic, cell_area=1.0)
...        .add_linear_benefit(carbon, name="carbon")
...        .add_area_target(50.0))
>>> sol = p.solve()
>>> round(sol.area, 6), sol.status
(50.0, 'optimal')

doc.x:
Every feature (species distribution, habitat, ecosystem service...) is
normalized to sum 1 and quantized to ``bits`` bits; the cells are then
ordered from the least to the most important by their marginal loss: the
loss to the features, weighted, of removing a cell at the point where it is
removed, with the other cells removed before it. Zonation iterates stable
sorts of the cells by that loss until the order is consistent (the mean
ranking error below ``ranking_error`` %). The result is the same, bit for
bit, as the z5 program (v2.4) on one thread.

terraflux.prioritize._zones.binary_stack.name: binary_stack
terraflux.prioritize._zones.binary_stack.summary: One 0 / 1 raster per zone from a raster of zone numbers (prioritizr's ``binary_stack()``): a mapping zone -> raster, ready for `add_locked_in_constraints()` (for example an existing zoning plan). ``zones``: the zones' names in the order of their numbers (default: those of a solution's ``zones`` map, else ``"1"``, ``"2"``, ...); cells with 0 or NaN are in no zone.

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> cost = tf.load_raster(tf.prioritize.example_data("cost"))
>>> features = tf.load_raster(tf.prioritize.example_data("features"))
>>> protected = tf.load_raster(tf.prioritize.example_data("protected"))
>>> p = (tf.prioritize.problem({"protect": cost, "use": cost * 0.4}, features, contribution={"use": 0.5})
...        .add_min_set_objective().add_relative_targets(0.3))
>>> existing = protected.fillna(0)              # the protected areas: zone 1 (protect)
>>> locked = tf.prioritize.binary_stack(existing, zones=p.zones)
>>> sorted(locked)
['protect', 'use']
>>> sol = p.add_locked_in_constraints(locked).solve()
>>> bool((sol.zones.values[existing.values == 1] == 1).all())
True

terraflux.redd.name: redd
terraflux.redd.summary: Verra's VT0007: the allocation of a jurisdiction's unplanned deforestation (UDef-A).

doc.x:
The steps of VT0007's Unplanned Deforestation Allocation as Clark Labs'
UDef-ARP implements them (GPL-3.0), the same numbers: the negligible risk
threshold of the distance to the forest's edge (`nrt()`), the vulnerability
in classes of geometric widths, the benchmark from that distance
(`benchmark()`) or an alternative map (`alternative()`), the relative
frequency of deforestation per class and subdivision and the density it gives
(`fit()`), that density in another period scaled to the activity data,
never above a cell (`allocate()`), and the predicted against the actual
deforestation in the cells of an assessment grid (`assess()`). As
Terraflux's ``redd.*`` operators.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    forest = tf.load_raster("forest_2015.tif")          # 1 forest
    cal = tf.load_raster("deforestation_2015_2020.tif") # 1 deforested in the calibration period
    juris = tf.load_raster("jurisdiction.tif")          # non-zero inside
    d = tf.redd.edge_distance(forest)
    t = tf.redd.nrt(d, cal, mask=juris)
    classes = tf.redd.benchmark(d, t, mask=juris)
    f = tf.redd.fit(classes, cal, subdivisions=tf.load_raster("states.tif"))
    a = tf.redd.allocate(classes_2020, f, expected=12_000)   # hectares of the activity data
    a.density                                             # hectares expected in each cell
    tf.redd.assess(a_cnf.density, cnf, grid_area=10_000, mask=juris).metrics

terraflux.restoration.name: restoration

doc.x:
This module reimplements GuidosToolbox (GTB) restoration tools:
- [`restoration_status()`][terraflux.restoration_status]: Evaluates landscape restoration status and metrics:
  Equivalent Connected Area (ECA), Degree of Coherence (DOC / COH), Restoration
  Potential (REST_POT), Relative Area of Connected Habitat (RAC), Average Patch
  Size (APS), and Critical New Object Area (CNOA).
- [`cost_distance()`][terraflux.cost_distance]: Anisotropic 8-neighbor cost distance transform across
  resistance friction surfaces.
- [`least_cost_path()`][terraflux.least_cost_path]: Two-ended least-cost corridor path between habitat markers.
- [`restoration_corridor()`][terraflux.restoration_corridor]: Comprehensive restoration corridor impact assessment
  evaluating connectivity gain (Delta-ECA, Delta-DOC) and restoration efficiency.

Vogt, P. & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis.
    European Journal of Remote Sensing, 50(1), 352-361. doi:10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650
Saura, S. & Pascual-Hortal, L. (2007). A new habitat availability index to integrate
    connectivity in landscape conservation planning. Landscape and Urban Planning, 83(2-3), 91-103.

terraflux.sdm.name: sdm
terraflux.sdm.summary: Species distribution modelling: preparing occurrences and predictors, fitting, projecting.

doc.x:
Most of the work in a species distribution model is preparing the data:
cleaning the occurrence records, thinning them, choosing the area the species
could reach, selecting predictors, sampling the background and splitting the
data into spatially independent folds. ``tf.sdm`` does each step with one
call and sensible defaults, every step remaining a public function with all
its options; the results feed scikit-learn directly. The steps reproduce the
R packages the field relies on (CoordinateCleaner, spThin, usdm, blockCV,
ENMeval, ecospat, predicts, maxnet), in C++ with OpenMP.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    occ = tf.load_vector(tf.sdm.example_data("bradypus"), crs="EPSG:4326")
    env = tf.load_raster(tf.sdm.example_data("bioclim"))

doc.x:
A model learns to tell the conditions where the species was found from
those available to it. Drawing the background from areas the species
never had access to (beyond a mountain range, on another continent) makes
the model learn geography instead of ecology and inflates its scores
(Barve et al. 2011, *Ecological Modelling* 222: 1810-1819). The
accessible area bounds the background sampling, the predictor selection
and the evaluation.

coordinate columns.

record (geodesic circles on the WGS 84 ellipsoid, merged);
``"convex_hull"``: the smallest convex polygon around the records,
widened by ``distance`` metres if given; ``"regions"``: the polygons of
``regions`` (ecoregions, biomes, watersheds) that hold at least one
record, widened by ``distance`` if given.
Polygons the result is cut to (a country, a continent, the land).
Vertices of each circle (``"buffer"``) or of the widening.

longitude / latitude in EPSG:4326).

terraflux.sdm._autocorrelation.autocorre.summary: The range of spatial autocorrelation of each predictor (and their median), in metres.

doc.x:
A variogram is fitted to a random sample of each band's cells (the
models tried by automap: spherical, exponential, Gaussian and Matern
with Stein's parameterisation over a range of smoothness, the one with
the smallest weighted squared error kept); its range parameter is how
far values stay alike. Spatial blocks for cross-validation should be
about as wide as the median range (Roberts et al. 2017; Valavi et al.
2019). As ``blockCV::cv_spatial_autocor``: the same sample (R's
generator, ``set.seed(seed)``) and variogram classes, and gstat's
Gauss-Newton fit step by step: the ranges agree to about 1e-6 (the
Matern model's derivative is numerical). Climate layers on a continent
often vary so smoothly that the fitted range exceeds the study area:
use the result as a guide, not blindly.

i: Metres per degree, for the block size on longitude / latitude grids.

``range`` (median, metres), ``block_size`` (the range in the units of
the grid: degrees on longitude / latitude) and ``layers`` (a table:
layer, range, sill, nugget, model, kappa).

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> env = tf.load_raster(tf.sdm.example_data("bioclim"))
>>> r = tf.sdm.autocorrelation_range(env.sel(band=["bio1", "bio12"]), n=1000, seed=1)
>>> round(r["range"] / 1000)      # km: temperature varies smoothly across the continent
226192
