doc.x:
Presence-only models (MaxEnt, presence-background regressions, machine
learning) contrast the presences with a sample of the cells the species
could have been found in. The sample is drawn as ``dismo::randomPoints``
draws it, with the same cells for the same seed: cells with a value in
every predictor, without replacement, on longitude / latitude grids
weighted by the cells' east-west width (so that each square kilometre
counts the same), leaving out the cells of the occurrences. Where to draw
from is the choice that matters most (Barve et al. 2011; VanDerWal et al.
2009): restrict it to the accessible area, to a distance band around the
records, or weight it by sampling effort.

data.

cells).

and they anchor ``distance`` and ``envelope``.

`accessible_area()`).

presences). ``dismo::randomPoints(prob = TRUE)``.

``(min, max)`` for cells farther than ``min`` and at most ``max``
(biomod2's "disk" pseudo-absences; longitude / latitude grids in
metres on the sphere, projected ones in their units).

0.025.

terraflux.sdm._bias.bias_surface.summary: Sampling effort as a surface: a Gaussian kernel density of the records of a group.

doc.x:
Records pile up where people look for species, near roads, towns and
research stations, and a presence-background model fitted to them
learns that bias along with the species' preferences. Drawing the
background with the same bias cancels it: the "target-group" background
of Phillips et al. (2009), whose effort is estimated from the records of
every species sampled the same way (the same taxonomic group, the same
collectors and decades). The density of those records, smoothed by a
Gaussian kernel, is the bias grid of Fourcade et al. (2014) and
Kramer-Schadt et al. (2013), the ``bias`` of `background()` (and
Maxent's "bias file").

The density is ``MASS::kde2d``'s, evaluated at the centres of the cells:
a product of two normal kernels whose standard deviations are
``bandwidth`` in x and in y. Note that ``kde2d(h = H)`` divides ``H`` by
4: it is ``bandwidth = H / 4`` here.

i:
The records of the target group (GeoDataFrame of points, or a table
with coordinate columns); reprojected to the CRS of ``env``.
The grid (a raster or a stack of predictors).

Standard deviation of the kernel, in the units of the CRS of ``env``
(metres on projected grids, degrees on longitude / latitude ones): a
number, a pair ``(x, y)`` or ``"nrd"``, the normal reference rule of
R's ``bw.nrd`` in each direction (``kde2d``'s default bandwidth).
The same bandwidth in both directions, the larger of the two.

``(min, max)``: bandwidths below / above them are raised / lowered to
them (either may be None). A floor keeps the surface of a clustered
group from collapsing onto its records; a ceiling keeps a widespread
one from flattening.

Non-negative weight of each record (e.g. the number of specimens or
visits); default 1.

``(lo, hi)``: map the densities linearly to ``[lo, hi]`` over the cells
kept, e.g. ``(0.05, 0.95)`` so that every cell keeps some chance of
being drawn. Default: the densities themselves (records per unit of
area of the CRS).

NaN on the cells without a value in every band of ``env`` (as
`background()` reads them); False: every cell of the grid.
Coordinate columns and CRS of a table of records.
Coordinate columns and CRS of a table of records.
Coordinate columns and CRS of a table of records.

``(y, x)`` on the grid of ``env``, named ``bias``; ``attrs`` hold the
bandwidths used (``bandwidth``) and the number of records (``n``).

doc.x:
Records without coordinates are left out; records outside the grid
count (their kernels reach into it), as in ``kde2d``. The sum runs over
the cells within 40 bandwidths of each record, beyond which the normal
density is 0 in double precision: the result is ``kde2d``'s up to
rounding.

Phillips, S. J. et al. (2009). Sample selection bias and presence-only
distribution models: implications for background and pseudo-absence
data. *Ecological Applications* 19: 181-197.

Fourcade, Y. et al. (2014). Mapping species distributions with MAXENT
using a geographically biased sample of presence data: a performance
assessment of methods for correcting sampling bias. *PLoS ONE* 9:
e97122.

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> env = tf.load_raster(tf.sdm.example_data("bioclim"))
>>> group = tf.load_table(tf.sdm.example_data("bradypus"))   # stands for the records of a whole group
>>> bias = tf.sdm.bias_surface(group, env, bandwidth=2.0, rescale=(0.05, 0.95))
>>> float(bias.min()), float(bias.max())
(0.05, 0.95)
>>> bg = tf.sdm.background(env, 1000, bias=bias, seed=1)

doc.x:
The tests of CoordinateCleaner (Zizka et al. 2019, *Methods in Ecology
and Evolution* 10: 744-751), the standard for GBIF data: records at
country or province centroids and capitals (coordinates filled in from
the name of a place), at biodiversity institutions (the address of a
museum or herbarium) or GBIF's headquarters, at 0/0 or with equal
longitude and latitude, in the sea, in towns, outside the country they
claim, far from the other records of their species, or duplicated.
Records without valid coordinates are always flagged (``invalid``).

Each test takes ``False`` (skip it), ``True`` (its defaults), a number
(its main option: a radius) or a dict of its options:

============== ========================================================================
test           options (defaults)
============== ========================================================================
equal          (none)
zeros          ``buffer`` 0.5 (degrees around 0/0)
capitals       ``buffer`` 10 000 m, ``geod`` True, ``ref`` None, ``verify`` False
centroids      ``buffer`` 1 000 m, ``detail`` "both" / "country" / "provinces",
               ``geod`` True, ``ref`` None, ``verify`` False
seas           ``scale`` 50 (Natural Earth land, 110 / 50 / 10), ``ref`` None
urban          ``ref`` None (Natural Earth urban areas)
countries      ``column`` (the records' country codes, required), ``ref`` None,
               ``ref_col`` None (``iso_a2_eh`` for two-letter codes, else ``iso_a3_eh``)
outliers       ``method`` "quantile" / "mad" / "distance", ``mltpl`` 5, ``tdi`` 1000 km,
               ``size`` 7 (species with more records are tested), ``min_occs`` 7
               (distinct locations), ``thinning`` False, ``thinning_res`` 0.5
gbif           ``buffer`` 1 000 m, ``geod`` True, ``verify`` False
institutions   ``buffer`` 100 m, ``geod`` False, ``ref`` None, ``verify`` False,
               ``verify_mltpl`` 10
duplicates     ``additions`` None (more columns that must also be equal)
aohi           ``buffer`` 10 000 m, ``geod`` True, ``taxa`` (Aves, Insecta, Mammalia, Plantae)
============== ========================================================================

``ref`` replaces the reference data (a table or GeoDataFrame of points, or
of polygons for seas / urban / countries); passing it in place of the
options also works (``seas=my_land``). The reference data are downloaded
on first use and cached (see `reference_data()`).

The results are CoordinateCleaner's (``clean_coordinates`` with the same
options), except where it errs: the zeros radius is in degrees as
documented (terra >= 1.8 made it 0.5 m), ``centroids`` "provinces"
selects the provinces, circles that cross the antimeridian or hold a pole
are drawn correctly, a record on a border between two countries is not
misaligned, the country codes are matched against ``iso_a3_eh`` /
``iso_a2_eh`` (with ``iso_a3`` France and Norway are "-99" and all their
records failed), species too small for the outlier test are not flagged,
the outlier test also runs on species with 10 000 records or more, and
institutions' ``verify`` works. Invalid coordinates are flagged instead of
stopping.

doc.x:
For moving windows of suitability, the ratio of the share of presences
to the share of available cells (background) predicted in the window;
the index is the rank correlation of that ratio with suitability: 1 for
a model whose higher predictions always hold relatively more presences,
0 for a random one. The standard metric for presence-only data (Boyce et
al. 2002; Hirzel et al. 2006). ``ecospat.boyce``, the same windows, ratios
and correlation, except for its "+1 trick": ecospat shifts its last window
by one unit of suitability, which removes that window for predictions on
0-1 and keeps it on 0-1000, so the index depends on the scale of the
predictions; here the last window is ``[max - width, max]`` on any scale.

i: Predictions at the background points (or every cell of the area).
0: moving windows (default); k > 0: k classes of equal width.

Width of the moving window (default: a tenth of the range of
``available``).
Ignore successive equal ratios in the correlation.

``cor`` (the index, rounded to 3 decimals as ecospat), ``f_ratio``
(predicted / expected ratios), ``hs`` (window centres) and ``used``
(the windows entering the correlation).

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> bg = rng.uniform(0, 1, 2000)
>>> pres = rng.beta(4, 1.5, 200)            # presences where suitability is high
>>> tf.sdm.boyce(pres, bg)["cor"]
0.954

doc.x:
Mesgaran et al. (2014, *Diversity and Distributions* 20: 1147-1159):
``NT1`` < 0 where some variable is outside its reference range (more
negative, farther out); inside every range, ``NT2`` is the Mahalanobis
distance to the reference centre relative to the largest one among the
reference points, > 1 for a combination of values the reference never
had. ``mic`` names the variable most responsible (1-based; 0 for analogue
conditions). The ``ExDet`` of the R package dsmextra, except that its
combinatorial ``mic`` pointed at the wrong variable (it numbered the
variables backwards).

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> env = tf.load_raster(tf.sdm.example_data("bioclim"))
>>> occ = tf.load_table(tf.sdm.example_data("bradypus"))
>>> data = tf.sdm.dataset(occ, tf.sdm.background(env, 2000, occ=occ, seed=1), env)
>>> out = tf.sdm.exdet(data, env.sel(band=["bio1", "bio12", "bio16"]))
>>> [str(b) for b in out.band.values]
['exdet', 'mic']

median; negative outside it, in percent of the range); the MESS is the
smallest over the variables, so negative values mark cells where at
least one variable is outside anything the model saw (Elith et al. 2010,
*Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 1: 330-342). ``predicts::mess``, the
same values.

area_of_habitat(

terraflux.sdm._habitat.area_of_habitat.summary: Area of habitat of species: their ranges refined by habitats and elevations.

doc.x:
The area of habitat (AOH; Brooks et al. 2019) of a species is the part
of its range covered by the land-cover classes it lives in, within its
elevation limits. With land cover given as shares of classes per cell
(as plangea's restoration model uses it), every cell of the range counts
for its area times the share of the species' natural classes. The
potential habitat is the same with the original vegetation, and the
gain map says how much habitat a species wins per unit of a cell
restored: what a restoration plan needs (plangea's ``harmonize_bd``).

i:
The species' ranges: a ``(band, y, x)`` raster whose band names are
the species (values above 0 inside the range), or a mapping or list
of named rasters.

The current share of every class in each cell (as
[`original_vegetation()`][terraflux.original_vegetation] takes it); NaN counts as 0.
The natural classes: a species' habitat is among them.

The classes each species lives in: a table of two columns (species,
class), a mapping species -> classes. Classes that are not natural
are left out.

The original vegetation: a [`OriginalVegetation`][terraflux.OriginalVegetation]
(its original cover gives the potential habitat, its restored
proportions and anthropic share the gain) or the original share of
every natural class (then restored land returns to those
proportions). Without it the potential habitat is the current one.
An elevation raster on the same grid.

A table with the species and their lower and upper elevations
(columns ``species``, ``lower``, ``upper``, or the first three
columns in that order); a missing limit is no limit. Cells without
an elevation stay in the range.

Species without a row in ``suitability`` live in every natural class
(True) or are left out (False, ``valid`` False).

The area of a cell: a number, a raster, or None: from the grid in km²
(see `cell_area_km2()`).

Also the habitat lost per unit of natural land converted (``loss``):
what conservation and conversion plans need.
The areas by species and the gain matrix.

doc.x:
The sums are plangea's, bit for bit: the shares of a species' classes
added in their order, times the cell's area, summed over its range in
R's 80-bit ``sum()``.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import xarray as xr
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> cover = xr.DataArray(np.array([[[0.6, 0.0]], [[0.2, 0.1]], [[0.2, 0.9]]]),
...                      dims=("band", "y", "x"), coords={"band": ["forest", "savanna", "crops"]})
>>> ranges = xr.DataArray(np.array([[[1.0, 1.0]], [[0.0, 1.0]]]),
...                       dims=("band", "y", "x"), coords={"band": ["toucan", "rhea"]})
>>> veg = tf.original_vegetation(cover, ["forest", "savanna"], ["crops"])
>>> aoh = tf.sdm.area_of_habitat(ranges, cover, ["forest", "savanna"], original=veg, cell_area=1.0,
...                              suitability={"toucan": ["forest"], "rhea": ["savanna"]})
>>> aoh.table[["species", "current", "potential"]].round(3)
  species  current  potential
0  toucan      0.6       0.75
1    rhea      0.1       1.00

doc.x:
Maxent (Phillips et al. 2006) as an infinitely weighted logistic
regression (Phillips et al. 2017): presences against background points
with the features of maxnet (linear ``l``, quadratic ``q``, product
``p``, hinge ``h``, threshold ``t``, categorical), maxnet's default
regularisation and glmnet's lasso path, keeping its last lambda. Every
step is a C++ port of R's maxnet 0.1.4 and glmnet 4.1-10 that gives R's
results bit for bit on x86-64 (coefficients, alpha, entropy, the four
output types with and without clamping), many times faster (hashing of
the duplicate rows, the gradient checks screened by a bound and run in
parallel, fused residual updates).

A scikit-learn classifier (``fit``, ``predict_proba``, ``predict``,
``decision_function``, ``get_params`` / ``set_params``, cloning and
pickling), usable in ``GridSearchCV`` and pipelines; scikit-learn itself
is not needed.

i:

doc.x:
MigClim 1.6's cellular automaton (Engler and Guisan 2009; Engler et al.
2012), the same run for a seed: in every dispersal step of every period,
a suitable empty cell is colonised from an occupied cell within the
kernel's distance with the kernel's probability at that distance (times
the source's propagule production while it matures, times the sink's
suitability), unless barriers lie between; long-distance dispersal sends
propagules to a random cell at a random distance; the cells that turn
unsuitable stay, temporarily resilient, until the period ends. Its random
numbers are Microsoft's C runtime ``rand()``, the one MigClim's Windows
builds draw from.

terraflux.sdm._predictors.select_predict.summary: Drop predictors that the others already explain (collinearity).

doc.x:
Climate layers are strongly correlated (the 19 bioclimatic variables
carry far fewer than 19 independent signals); collinear predictors make
a model's coefficients unstable and its projections to new conditions
unreliable (Dormann et al. 2013, *Ecography* 36: 27-46). Two filters of
the R package usdm, with the same results:

- ``cor`` (usdm's ``vifcor``): while the most correlated pair has
  ``|r| >= cor``, drop the one of the two with the larger VIF;
- ``vif`` (usdm's ``vifstep``): while the largest VIF is ``>= vif``, drop
  that variable.

With both, the correlation filter runs first. Variables in ``keep`` are
never dropped. Where usdm errs, the correct form: the loops stop when
one variable (or only kept ones) remains instead of failing, names with
spaces work, rasters of 7000-10 000 cells are sampled at random (terra
took their first cells) and tables are sampled from 7000 rows on in both
filters (usdm's ``vifstep`` already from 6000).

i: Raster stack (band, y, x) or a table with one column per predictor.
VIF threshold (usdm's default 10; 5 is stricter); None: no VIF filter.
Correlation threshold (e.g. 0.7); None: no correlation filter.
Names of predictors to keep whatever their collinearity.

Polygons the raster is cut to first: collinearity in the accessible
area, not in the whole raster.

Cells sampled from rasters of 7000 cells or more (usdm's 5000; None:
all cells).
Seed of R's generator for the sample (default random).

The predictors kept (the same type as ``env``), with
``attrs["selection"]``: the variables excluded in order, the VIF of
the kept ones and the seed.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> env = tf.load_raster(tf.sdm.example_data("bioclim"))
>>> kept = tf.sdm.select_predictors(env, vif=10, seed=1)
>>> [str(b) for b in kept.band.values]
['bio5', 'bio7', 'bio8', 'bio16', 'bio17']
>>> kept.attrs["selection"]["excluded"]
['bio1', 'bio6', 'bio9', 'bio12']

terraflux.sdm._thin.thin.summary: Thin occurrence records so that no two kept records are closer than ``distance``.

doc.x:
Records cluster where people sample (near roads, towns, universities),
and a model fitted to them learns that bias along with the species'
preferences. Thinning removes records until the remaining ones are at
least ``distance`` apart while keeping as many as possible: the
randomised heuristic of spThin (Aiello-Lammens et al. 2015, *Ecography*
38: 541-545), which repeatedly drops a record with the most neighbours
(a random one among ties) and keeps the best of ``reps`` repetitions.
The same records as ``spThin::thin`` for the same seed; distances on a
sphere of radius 6378.388 km, as spThin's ``fields::rdist.earth``.

Occurrence records: GeoDataFrame of points, or a table with
coordinate columns.
Minimum distance between kept records, in metres.

Repetitions of the heuristic; the one keeping the most records is
returned (the first among equals). More repetitions keep more records,
rarely many more beyond 10-100.

Seed of R's generator (``set.seed``); default random (recorded in
``attrs["thin"]``).

longitude / latitude in EPSG:4326).

the seed and the number of records each repetition kept. Records
without coordinates are always kept (they have no neighbours): drop
them first with `clean_occurrences()`.

terraflux.sensitivity.name: sensitivity
terraflux.sensitivity.summary: Global sensitivity analysis: Morris's elementary effects and Sobol's indices, as SALib computes them.

doc.x:
`design()` gives the runs (Morris's trajectories, or Saltelli's runs of a
scrambled Sobol' sequence), `evaluate()` runs a model at each of them (on
this computer, or on the helpers of [`parallel`][terraflux.parallel]), and
`analyze()` turns the outputs into the indices. The designs and the indices
are SALib 1.6's (MIT), the same numbers; the same as Terraflux's
``sensitivity.*`` operators.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    d = tf.sensitivity.design("sobol", {"rate": [0.01, 0.1], "threshold": [0.2, 0.8]}, n=256)
    y = tf.sensitivity.evaluate(lambda p: model(rate=p[0], threshold=p[1]), d)
    s = tf.sensitivity.analyze(d, y)
    s.indices                                  # S1, ST and their intervals by factor

    # a terraflux tool, its runs spread over the helpers of this computer's group
    f = tf.parallel.call("surface.gravity", sources, exponent=tf.parallel.param(0))
    y = tf.sensitivity.evaluate(f, d, on=tf.helpers(), summary=np.mean)

Morris: μ, μ* (the mean absolute elementary effect: the importance) and σ
(interactions and non-linearity), with μ*'s bootstrap interval. Sobol: the
first order (S1: the share of the output's variance due to the factor
alone), total (ST: with its interactions) and second order (S2: of pairs)

...                           n=1024, seed=11)
>>> ishigami = lambda p: np.sin(p[0]) + 7 * np.sin(p[1]) ** 2 + 0.1 * p[2] ** 4 * np.sin(p[0])
>>> s = tf.sensitivity.analyze(d, tf.sensitivity.evaluate(ishigami, d))
>>> s.indices[["s1", "st"]].round(2)          # the exact values: 0.31 0.44 0 / 0.56 0.44 0.24

terraflux.services.name: services
terraflux.services.summary: Ecosystem services: the models of InVEST, reimplemented.

doc.x:
Ports of the Natural Capital Project's InVEST models (natcap.invest, Apache-2.0),
computed in C++ with OpenMP from terraflux's data objects: their maps, bit for
bit where the arithmetic permits, from land use maps and parameter tables.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    lulc = tf.load_raster("lulc_2020.tif")
    pools = tf.load_table("carbon_pools.csv")
    c = tf.services.carbon(lulc, pools, future=tf.load_raster("lulc_2050.tif"))
    c.totals                                   # tons of carbon, and the change

    hq = tf.services.habitat_quality(lulc, threats, sensitivity, threat_maps, half_saturation=0.05)
    hq.quality["current"]

    wy = tf.services.water_yield(lulc, biophysical, rain, et0, soil_depth, pawc, seasonality=5,
                                 watersheds=tf.load_vector("watersheds.gpkg"))
    wy.watersheds                              # mean yield and volume per watershed

    nd = tf.services.ndr(dem, lulc, runoff_proxy, nutrients_table, watersheds, threshold=1000,
                         subsurface_critical_length=200, subsurface_efficiency=0.8)
    nd.watersheds                              # nitrogen and phosphorus exports per watershed

    bees = tf.services.pollination(lulc, guilds, biophysical, farms=tf.load_vector("farms.gpkg"))
    bees.abundance["apis"]["spring"], bees.farms   # abundance by species and season, farm yields

    swy = tf.services.seasonal_water_yield(dem, lulc, swy_biophysical, watersheds, threshold=1000,
                                           precipitation=monthly_rain, et0=monthly_et0, soil_group=soils,
                                           rain_events=[12, 10, 9, 6, 4, 2, 1, 1, 3, 6, 9, 11])
    swy.baseflow                               # the recharge that reaches the streams (mm / yr)

    cv = tf.services.coastal_vulnerability(aoi, landmass, wwiii, bathymetry, shelf, dem, habitats,
                                           model_resolution=250, max_fetch_distance=12000,
                                           dem_averaging_radius=1000)
    cv.exposure                                # exposure index of the shore points, with and without habitats

    em = tf.services.emissions(tf.load_raster("lulc_2000_2010_2020.tif"), {1: 150, 2: 10, 3: 40},
                               regrowth={3: {"max": 120, "rate": 0.05}})
    em.periods                                 # emissions and removals of land change, t CO2 per period

terraflux.services._coastal.coastal_vuln.summary: Exposure of the coast to erosion and flooding (InVEST's coastal vulnerability model).

doc.x:
Shore points are spaced ``model_resolution`` apart along the coast of the
landmass inside the area of interest; each gets a rank from 1 (sheltered) to 5
(exposed) for every hazard: wind and waves (16 fetch rays cast from the point
up to ``max_fetch_distance`` or the land they hit; the relative exposure index
``REI = sum F_k pct_k V_k`` and the wave power, the larger of the ocean waves
(along rays that reach the maximum fetch) and the waves the local wind raises
(from the fetch, the mean depth along the ray and the wind speed), from the Wave
Watch III points), surge potential (distance to the continental shelf contour),
relief (mean elevation within ``dem_averaging_radius``), habitats (each one
within its protection distance lowers ``R_hab`` from 5), and optionally
geomorphology (the mean rank of the lines within half the model resolution)
and sea-level rise. Continuous variables become ranks by their quintiles over
the points (relief reversed). The exposure index is the geometric mean of the
ranks; without habitats, with ``R_hab = 5``; the difference is the role of
the habitats. Optionally, the population density around each point.

The outputs are InVEST's (natcap.invest 3.20), bit for bit, also for inputs
in other CRS (``tests/test_services_coastal.py``), with two
corrections: InVEST drops the edges of the landmass whose ends are
``numpy.isclose(..., rtol=1e-7)``, meant for repeated vertices, but relative to
the coordinates (at UTM northings of 8e6, edges up to 0.8 m long), which
breaks the coastline there: here only edges of length 0 are left out; and for
a fetch ray with no valid depth InVEST widens a window around its end, moving
it instead of cutting it where it meets the top or left edge of the raster:
here the window is the square around the end, cut at the edges. Where a ray
meets several edges of the land, its end is the nearest intersection with
the whole ray (InVEST shortens the ray edge by edge, in the order of its
R-tree, so its end may differ in the last bits, ~1e-8 m; REI and the local
waves carry that, ~1e-11 relative). Inputs in other CRS are reprojected as
InVEST does: vectors by GDAL's coordinate transformation, rasters by GDAL's
warp (bilinear, its approximate transformation of 1/8 cell).

Polygons of the area of interest, in a projected CRS in metres (the CRS of
the results).
Polygons of the land (any CRS); their holes (lakes) are not coast.

Wave Watch III points with, for each sector ``<deg>`` of 0, 22, 45, ...,
337: ``REI_PCT<deg>``, ``REI_V<deg>``, ``WavP_<deg>``, ``WavPPCT<deg>`` and
``V10PCT_<deg>``.

Spacing of the shore points (m); also the cell size of rasters in
longitude / latitude once projected.
Radius (m) of the mean elevation around the points.

Lines with a ``RANK`` field (1 to 5) and the rank of points with no line
within half the model resolution.

terraflux.services._habitat.habitat_qual.summary: Habitat degradation, quality and rarity (InVEST's habitat quality model).

doc.x:
Each threat (crops, roads, towns...) degrades the habitat around it: its
impact decays linearly or exponentially with the distance to the nearest
cell of the threat, up to its maximum distance (exponentially: to 5 % there),
and weighs by its relative weight, by the sensitivity of the cell's land use
class to it and by the cell's access (legal protection). The degradation
D of a cell is the sum over the threats; its quality is
``h (1 - D^z / (D^z + k^z))``, h the habitat suitability of its class, k the
half-saturation constant and z = 2.5. With a base map, the rarity of each
class of the current (and future) map: ``1 - n_x / (n_base + n_x)``, the
cell counts in the two maps.

The maps are InVEST's (natcap.invest 3.20, which takes the distance to the
nearest threat cell since 3.12): the same distance transform in float32 and
the same float32 expressions, bit for bit (the exponential decay through
numpy's float32 ``exp``, as InVEST computes it).

i: The current land use map (integer codes; projected, in metres).

(metres), ``weight`` (relative) and ``decay`` (``"linear"`` or
``"exponential"``).

A DataFrame by land use class (``lucode``): ``habitat`` (0 to 1) and a

doc.x:
The nitrogen and phosphorus loads of each land use (scaled by the runoff
proxy over its mean) split into a surface part and, for nitrogen, a dissolved
subsurface part. The surface load reaches a stream in the share
``NDR = (1 - eff') / (1 + exp((IC_0 - IC) / k))``: ``eff'`` the retention of
the cells it crosses on its way down (each land use's maximum efficiency
reached over its critical length), ``IC = log10(D_up / D_dn)`` the index of
connectivity of the slope (Borselli et al. 2008) and ``IC_0`` half way between
its lowest and highest values. The subsurface load reaches it in the share
``1 - eff_sub (1 - exp(-5 l / l_sub))``, ``l`` the distance down to the stream.

The rasters are InVEST's (natcap.invest 3.20) bit for bit, in its float32 and
float64 types: the DEM filled, routed (pygeoprocessing's multiple flow
directions or D8) and traced into streams as pygeoprocessing does, its percent
slope and the effective retention; the watershed totals agree to float32
precision. One correction: InVEST measures the distance to the stream of the
subsurface delivery in cells against a critical length in metres; here it is in
metres (cells x cell size).

annual precipitation, any units).

retention efficiency, 0 to 1), ``crit_len_n`` (m) and
``proportion_subsurface_n``; for phosphorus the same columns ending in

the inputs to them), and the totals are given per polygon.

The rasters may be on different grids (cells, extent, CRS): as InVEST does,
they are put on the DEM's cells first, by the nearest cell, over the
intersection of their bounds and the watersheds' (its corner moved onto the
DEM's cells), so the maps cover the watersheds' box only.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import geopandas as gpd
>>> from affine import Affine
>>> from shapely.geometry import box
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> y, x = np.mgrid[:40, :50]
>>> z = (100 + 0.5 * x + 8 * np.sin(y / 5.0)).astype("float32")      # a slope with ridges
>>> t = Affine(30, 0, 500000, 0, -30, 8000000)
>>> dem = tf.load_raster(tf.write_raster(z, "ndr_dem.tif", crs="EPSG:31983", transform=t))
>>> lulc = dem.copy(data=np.where(x < 25, 1, 2).astype("int16"))    # forest, crops
>>> rain = dem.copy(data=np.full(z.shape, 1200, "float32"))
>>> bio = pd.DataFrame({"lucode": [1, 2], "load_n": [2.0, 40.0], "load_type_n": "measured-runoff",
...                     "eff_n": [0.8, 0.2], "crit_len_n": [150.0, 30.0], "proportion_subsurface_n": [0.1, 0.4],
...                     "load_p": [0.1, 3.0], "load_type_p": "measured-runoff", "eff_p": [0.8, 0.3],
...                     "crit_len_p": [150.0, 30.0]})
>>> ws = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"ws_id": [1]}, geometry=[box(*dem.rio.bounds())], crs=dem.rio.crs)
>>> r = tf.services.ndr(dem, lulc, rain, bio, ws, threshold=50, subsurface_critical_length=200,
...                     subsurface_efficiency=0.8)
>>> crops, forest = np.nanmean(r.n_total_export.values[:, 30:]), np.nanmean(r.n_total_export.values[:, :20])
>>> bool(crops > 10 * forest)                     # crops export far more nitrogen (kg / ha / yr)

doc.x:
Wild bees nest where the land offers their nesting substrates and fly to
the flowers around (Lonsdorf et al. 2009). For each species ``s``: its
habitat nesting index ``HN = max_n N_n ns_n`` (the availability of each
substrate in the cell's land use class times the species' use of it); the
flowers it forages on in each season, ``FF_j = RA_j fa_j`` (floral resources
of the class times its relative activity in the season), summed over the
seasons; the floral resources within its flight range ``FR``, that sum
convolved with an exponential decay kernel of mean distance ``alpha`` (out
to 5 alpha, normalized over the cells of the map); the supply
``PS = sa HN FR`` (``sa``: its relative abundance); and its abundance in each
season, ``PA_j = FF_j / FR conv(PS)``. With farms, their own floral
resources and nesting replace the land's, and each farm gets the on-farm
wild pollinator abundance ``PAT (1 - h) / (h (1 - 2 PAT) + PAT)`` (``h`` its
crop's half saturation, in its season), the yield index of all pollinators
``min(managed + wild, 1)`` and its wild part, averaged over the farm.

The maps are InVEST's (natcap.invest 3.20), bit for bit: the kernels and
the convolutions as pygeoprocessing makes them (256 x 256 blocks of the map
and of the kernel, each pair by numpy's FFT, the same transforms, added up
in float32), with one correction: pygeoprocessing zeroes the values of a
block's convolution within 1e-8 of 1e-8 instead of within 1e-8 of 0, as it
documents (here, of 0). The farm means agree to float32 precision (InVEST
sums the cells in float32).

i: Land use map (integer codes; projected, in metres).

A DataFrame with a row per species (``species``): ``alpha`` (mean flight
distance, metres), ``relative_abundance``, a
``nesting_suitability_<substrate>_index`` column per nesting substrate and a
``foraging_activity_<season>_index`` column per season (0 to 1).

A DataFrame by land use class (``lucode``): ``nesting_<substrate>_
availability_index`` and ``floral_resources_<season>_index`` (0 to 1), for
the substrates and seasons of the guild table.

Optional farm polygons (GeoDataFrame): ``crop_type``, ``season`` (when the
crop is pollinated), ``half_sat`` (the wild pollinator abundance that gives
half the pollinator-dependent yield), ``p_dep`` (share of the yield that
depends on pollinators), ``p_managed`` (share of pollination by managed
pollinators), and the farm's own ``fr_<season>`` and ``n_<substrate>``.
Value marking missing cells in the land use map.

Also keep the intermediate maps (the substrates and floral resources, the
habitat nesting, foraged flowers, foraging effectiveness, floral resources
and convolved supply of every species, the kernels, the farm rasters).

terraflux.services._swy.seasonal_water_y.summary: Quickflow, local recharge and baseflow by month and year (InVEST's seasonal water yield model).

doc.x:
The quickflow of each month is the SCS curve number runoff of its storms
(``QF = 25.4 n ((a - S) e^(-0.2 S/a) + S^2/a e^(0.8 S/a) E1(S/a))``, ``a`` the
rain of a storm in inches, ``S = 1000 / CN - 10``, all the rain on the
streams). The local recharge is the rain that is not quickflow nor evaporated,
``L = P - QF - AET``, with the monthly ``AET = min(Kc ET0, P - QF + alpha_m
beta L_sum_avail)``: the cell can use water from upslope, the available
recharge ``L_avail = min(gamma L, L)`` of the cells above, summed by their
shares of the flow. The baseflow is the part of the recharge that reaches a
stream: ``B_sum`` along the flow from the outlets up and ``B = max(B_sum L /
L_sum, 0)``.

The rasters are InVEST's (natcap.invest 3.20) bit for bit, in its float32 and
float64 types: the DEM filled, routed (pygeoprocessing's multiple flow
directions or D8) and traced into streams as pygeoprocessing does, the
quickflow, curve numbers, recharge and baseflow; the polygon sums agree to
float32 precision (InVEST adds the cells in float32). Five bugs of InVEST
are corrected (and the tests compare against InVEST with them corrected):
cells without recharge add none to the baseflow (InVEST reads their nodata
as numbers, which makes the baseflow infinite there and upslope),
``L_sum_avail`` sums the upslope terms by their shares of the flow (InVEST
takes their mean weighted by the raw flow weights, so a cell fed by three
cells gets the mean of their recharge instead of the sum), the flow off the
raster ends the baseflow path as the flow into a hole of the DEM does
(InVEST gives such an outlet ``B_sum = 0``), a cell without elevation that a
D8 direction points into gets no recharge, and fractional curve numbers are
kept with integer land use and soil maps (InVEST truncates them).

doc.x:
The rasters may be on different grids (cells, extent, CRS): as InVEST does,
they are put on the DEM's cells first, by the nearest cell, over the
intersection of their bounds and the watersheds' (its corner moved onto the
DEM's cells), so the maps cover the watersheds' box only.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> import geopandas as gpd
>>> from affine import Affine
>>> from shapely.geometry import box
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> y, x = np.mgrid[:40, :50]
>>> z = (100 + 0.6 * x + 6 * np.sin(y / 6.0)).astype("float32")
>>> t = Affine(30, 0, 500000, 0, -30, 8000000)
>>> dem = tf.load_raster(tf.write_raster(z, "swy_dem.tif", crs="EPSG:31983", transform=t))
>>> lulc = dem.copy(data=np.where(x < 25, 1, 2).astype("int16"))       # forest, pasture
>>> soil = dem.copy(data=np.full(z.shape, 2, "uint8"))                  # group B
>>> bio = pd.DataFrame({"lucode": [1, 2], "cn_a": [30, 49], "cn_b": [55, 69], "cn_c": [70, 79],
...                     "cn_d": [77, 84], **{f"kc_{m}": [1.0, 0.8] for m in range(1, 13)}})
>>> rain = [dem.copy(data=np.full(z.shape, v, "float32")) for v in [250, 220, 180, 90, 40, 20,
...                                                                   10, 15, 50, 120, 180, 230]]
>>> et0 = [dem.copy(data=np.full(z.shape, 110, "float32"))] * 12
>>> ws = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"ws_id": [1]}, geometry=[box(*dem.rio.bounds())], crs=dem.rio.crs)
>>> s = tf.services.seasonal_water_yield(dem, lulc, bio, ws, threshold=60, precipitation=rain, et0=et0,
...                                      soil_group=soil, rain_events=[12, 11, 9, 6, 3, 2, 1, 1, 3, 7, 10, 12])
>>> land, qf = s.stream.values == 0, s.quickflow.values               # mm / yr (all the rain on streams)
>>> bool(qf[land & (x > 30)].mean() > 3 * qf[land & (x < 20)].mean())  # pasture runs off more than forest
True
>>> list(s.watersheds.columns)
['ws_id', 'geometry', 'qb', 'vri_sum', 'geom_id']

actual evapotranspiration over precipitation

volume; with a demand table, the consumption and the realized supply; with
a valuation table, the hydropower energy and its net present value.

terraflux.simulate.name: simulate
terraflux.simulate.summary: Land use and land cover change: analysis, transition potential, allocation, validation.

doc.x:
``tf.simulate`` brings together what the land change models of the field
do, as interchangeable pieces of one model: how much changes (Markov chains,
area demands as in CLUE-S, demands for goods and services as in CLUMondo),
where change is likely (weights of evidence, logistic regression, any
scikit-learn estimator), the rules of change (allowed conversions,
elasticities, succession, adaptive inertia) and the shape of the new patches
(CLUE-S allocation, Dinamica EGO's Expander and Patcher, PLUS's multi-type
random patch seeds, FUTURES' patch growing). The reference implementations
(lulcc, CLUMondo, r.futures, MOLUSCE, OpenLand, diffeR) are reproduced bit
for bit where their code is open; Dinamica EGO and PLUS are implemented from
their publications.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    lu = tf.load_raster(tf.simulate.example_data("pie_landuse"))   # 1985, 1991, 1999
    ch = tf.simulate.changes(lu)                                   # transitions, areas, intensity
    ch.intensity(gain=2, loss=1)                                   # Aldwaik & Pontius
    tf.simulate.difference_components(ch.matrix())                 # quantity, exchange, shift
    tf.simulate.Markov.from_maps(lu[0], lu[2], steps=14).multi     # rates per year

terraflux.simulate._continuous.Continuou.name: ContinuousPatcher
terraflux.simulate._continuous.Continuou.sig:
ContinuousPatcher(
    mean: float = 1.0,
    variance: float = 0.0,
    isometry: float = 1.0,
    unit: str = 'hectares',
    prune_factor: float = 10.0,
    window: tuple = (3, 3),
)
terraflux.simulate._continuous.Continuou.summary: New patches that take a stock (biomass, carbon, timber) up to a quota.

doc.x:
Dinamica EGO's ``PatcherContinuousState``: the Patcher of a continuous
state. Each patch seed is drawn among the cells with stock and
probability, the patch grows to a lognormal size, every cell of it gives
all its stock, and patches are made until the stock taken reaches the
quota.

- Candidates: the cells with stock > 0 and probability > 0 ranked from
  the highest probability; the first ones kept while their summed stock
  is at most ``prune_factor x quota``.
- Seeds: drawn from those without replacement in proportion to the
  probability (measured in Dinamica EGO 8.13). The list is not ranked
  again when it runs out: the quota is then left unmet.
- Patches: lognormal size of the given mean and variance; each new cell
  drawn among the cells with stock around the patch in proportion to
  ``P x isometry^k``, ``k`` the patch cells in its window (as
  [`ExpanderPatcher`][terraflux.simulate.ExpanderPatcher]); a patch stops as soon as the quota is met,
  so the last cell may exceed it.

i: Mean and variance of the patch sizes, in ``unit``.
Mean and variance of the patch sizes, in ``unit``.

0 leaves single cells, 1 follows the probabilities, 2 makes compact
patches (0-2).

Units of the patch sizes and of the stock's area: Dinamica's stock
per hectare and sizes in hectares (from the map's cell area in square
metres), or per cell and in cells, or per map area unit and in map
area units.

How much more stock than the quota the ranked cells hold (Dinamica's
10).
The neighbour window of patch growth (rows, columns), odd.

doc.x:
Dinamica's functor crashes for patches of more than one cell (as its
Patcher does), so the candidates, the pruning, the seed draw and the
quota were measured with one-cell patches; the patch growth is the
published Patcher's. Its random numbers depend on more than its seed
(the same run in another folder differs), so the comparison is
statistical.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> biomass = np.full((20, 20), 9.0)           # per cell
>>> p = rng.random((20, 20))
>>> cp = tf.simulate.ContinuousPatcher(mean=4, variance=1, isometry=1.5, unit="cells")
>>> a = cp.allocate(biomass, p, quota=100, seed=1)
>>> a.n_cells, a.remaining
(12, -8.0)

doc.x:
After the development of each step, a flood may strike each catchment:
with probability ``max`` (the largest flood probability of the
catchment's cells, or of the depth maps), at a probability ``p`` drawn
uniformly. Its depth at each cell comes from the depth maps of the
probabilities (the map of the largest probability below ``p``) or, from
flood probability maps, as the HAND percentile of the cells flooded at
``p`` minus the cell's HAND. The damage is the depth-damage curve's (%)
unless the cell was adapted to such floods; a damaged developed cell
then retreats (abandoned, its demand moved to a subregion drawn from the
redistribution matrix, scaled by the population densities), adapts
(protected up to the return period of the flood) or stays, from its
adaptive capacity and the response lines, perturbed by a Gaussian.

terraflux.simulate._molusce.MolusceCA.name: MolusceCA
terraflux.simulate._molusce.MolusceCA.summary: MOLUSCE's simulator: each iteration makes the observed transitions where the model is most confident.

doc.x:
At each iteration the potential predicts every cell's transition and
its confidence ([`MolusceWoE`][terraflux.simulate._molusce.MolusceWoE], or any potential with a layer per
class: the class of largest potential, confidence ``100 x`` the gap to
the second); then, for each pair of classes in order, the ``n`` cells
(the demand: the cross table of the observed change, the same every
iteration) predicted to take that transition with the highest
confidence plus ``U(0, 1) / 1000`` change.

The random numbers are numpy's legacy generator (``RandomState(seed)``),
as MOLUSCE draws them after ``numpy.random.seed(seed)``. Among cells of
equal confidence and draw (which the 1/1000 rarely leaves), the later
cells change first (MOLUSCE leaves the order to numpy's quicksort).

terraflux.simulate._molusce.MolusceWoE.name: MolusceWoE
terraflux.simulate._molusce.MolusceWoE.sig: MolusceWoE(bins: dict | None = None, unit_cell: float = 1)
terraflux.simulate._molusce.MolusceWoE.summary: MOLUSCE's weights of evidence (``WoeManager``): one model per transition, persistence included.

doc.x:
Each factor is cut into categories (``bins``: ``(-inf, b0) -> 1``,
``[b0, b1) -> 2``... ``[bn, inf) -> n + 2``; or its integer values
themselves); for each transition code observed between the two maps
(the cells that went from ``i`` to ``j``, ``i == j`` included), every
category gets ``W+ + sum(W-) - W-`` over the factor's categories (halved
with two categories), and a cell's total weight is the sum over the
factors. A cell of class ``i`` is predicted to take the transition
``i -> j`` of largest total weight; its confidence is ``100 x
(sigmoid(largest) - sigmoid(second largest))``, truncated.

i:
``{driver: [bounds]}`` (sorted); drivers not named are used as
integer categories.
MOLUSCE's unit cell (areas in unit cells).

doc.x:
MOLUSCE keeps the largest weight seen *before* the largest as the
second, which depends on the order of the classes: here the second
largest weight (tested against MOLUSCE with ``tools/molusce_fixed.patch``).
MOLUSCE also stores the factors as 8-bit integers, wrapping integer
categories outside 0-255 and truncating fractions; here integer
categories keep their values and fractional values need bins.

terraflux.simulate._patches.ExpanderPatc.sig:
ExpanderPatcher(
    expansion: object = 0.5,
    expander: object = (1.0, 0.0, 1.0),
    patcher: object = (1.0, 0.0, 1.0),
    size_unit: str = 'cells',
    prune_factor: float = 10.0,
    window: tuple = (3, 3),
    steps: int | None = None,
)
terraflux.simulate._patches.ExpanderPatc.summary: Dinamica's Expander and Patcher allocation of transitions (``AllocateTransitions``).

doc.x:
Each step, the changes of a transition are ``round(rate x cells of the
origin class)`` (the demand's rates, e.g. a [`Markov`][terraflux.simulate.Markov] chain); a
share ``expansion`` goes to the Expander, the rest (and what the
Expander could not place) to the Patcher.

- Expander: a cell's probability becomes ``P`` where at least 5 cells of
  its 3 x 3 window hold the target class, else ``P n_j / 5`` (Dinamica
  EGO 8, measured; Soares-Filho et al. 2002 give ``n_j / 4`` from 4).
  The cells are ranked, the first ``prune_factor x changes`` kept, drawn
  in proportion to that probability and each tried once: a seed with
  that probability.
- Patcher: seeds drawn in proportion to the probability among the first
  ``prune_factor x changes`` cells, until its changes are made.
- Each seed grows a patch of lognormal size (mean, variance) cell by
  cell, each new cell drawn among the origin-class cells around the
  patch in proportion to ``P x isometry^k``, ``k`` the patch cells in its
  window: isometry 0 leaves single cells, 1 follows the probabilities,
  2 makes compact patches.

i:
Share of the changes made by the Expander (one value or
``{(from, to): share}``).

``(mean, variance, isometry)`` of the patches (one tuple or per
transition), the sizes in ``size_unit``.

``(mean, variance, isometry)`` of the patches (one tuple or per
transition), the sizes in ``size_unit``.

``"cells"``, ``"hectares"`` (Dinamica's: from the map's cell area in
square metres) or ``"area"`` (the map's area units).
How many cells per change are ranked for the draw (Dinamica's 10).

Steps to simulate (default: the demand's ``steps``, e.g. a Markov
chain's).

doc.x:
The functors of Dinamica EGO 8.13 crash for patches of more than one
cell, so only their seed selection could be measured (Expander:
acceptance ``n_j / 5`` per cell and the draw by probability, from
12 x 5000 trials; Patcher: the draw by probability among the pruned
cells); the patch growth follows the published descriptions.

doc.x:
Each step, CARS iterates from the current map until every class has the
cells the demand asks for. In an iteration, each free cell ``i`` gives
each class ``k`` the overall probability

- ``OP = P(i,k) x Omega(i,k) x D(k)``, ``Omega = w(k) x`` the cells of
  ``k`` in the ``window x window`` neighbourhood (the centre left out)
  over ``window^2 - 1``;
- where ``Omega = 0``, a random seed: ``OP = P x (r x mu(k)) x D`` when a
  uniform ``r < P``, else 0;

a roulette wheel over ``OP`` picks a class ``c``, and the cell turns to
``c`` when ``P(i,c) > tau`` and the conversion is allowed;
``tau = decay^l x r``, ``r`` normal of mean 1 in [0, 2], ``l`` raised by
one after each iteration that cut the total gap to the demand by less
than ``step_size`` cells. ``D(k)`` starts at 1 and grows while the
class's shortage grows (shrinks while its excess grows).

The growth probabilities ``P`` come from the model's potential (one
layer per class, as an [`Estimator`][terraflux.simulate.Estimator] with ``target="expansion"``
gives: PLUS's LEAS); the demand is an [`AreaDemand`][terraflux.simulate.AreaDemand] or a
[`Markov`][terraflux.simulate.Markov] chain projected from the starting map (PLUS's default);
the rules give the conversions allowed (``allowed``, 0/1, rows the
current class) and the restricted cells (``restrictions``).

i:
Neighbourhood weight ``w(k)`` of each class, 0 to 1 (a number for
all or ``{class: weight}``; default 1).

Patch generation threshold ``mu(k)`` of each class, 0 to 1 (the
paper's 0.1): how strongly random seeds compete with the growth of
existing patches.
Decay factor ``delta`` of the threshold, in (0, 1] (the paper's 0.9).

Gap reduction (cells per iteration) below which the threshold
decays (PLUS's "Step"; the paper's 500).
Side of the neighbourhood, odd (3 = the Moore neighbourhood).
Iterations per step before giving up (the map is kept as it is).

doc.x:
From the paper alone (PLUS has no source code): the standard deviation
of the threshold's normal ``r`` is not given (here 1/3, values outside
[0, 2] drawn again); the changes proposed in an iteration are made in a
random order, a class taking no cell once it has its demand and losing
none while it has no more than its demand (the paper does not say how a
class is held at its demand). The random numbers of a cell come from a
hash of (seed, step, iteration, cell): the same seed gives the same
simulation with any number of threads.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> S = tf.simulate
>>> land = np.ones((40, 40)); land[15:25, 15:25] = 2
>>> p = S.RasterPotential({1: np.full((40, 40), 0.1), 2: np.full((40, 40), 0.8)})
>>> demand = S.AreaDemand(np.array([[1500, 100], [1400, 200]]), classes=[1, 2])
>>> sim = S.Model(p, demand, S.CARS()).run(land, seed=1)
>>> int((sim.maps[-1] == 2).sum())
200

doc.x:
The map is cut into ``quadrants = (horizontal, vertical)`` parts (the
columns into ``horizontal``, the rows into ``vertical``); in each, up to
``per_quadrant`` cells are drawn in proportion to their attraction
(cells of attraction <= 0 or missing never); a draw closer than

doc.x:
Dinamica EGO 8.13 gives each quadrant ``n // q`` rows or columns (the
last ``n % q`` never get a destination) and draws an integer of the
summed attraction with rounding (the first cell of a quadrant gets half
its share, and a draw past the end takes the quadrant's last cell even
with no attraction, about 1 / (2 x summed attraction) of the time).
Here the quadrants cover the map (``floor(k n / q)`` boundaries) and
the draw is in exact proportion to the attraction.

i:
Conversion matrix, rows the current class, columns the next (a
DataFrame named by class, or an array in the model's class order):
``1`` allowed, ``0`` not; ``-1`` the cell may leave its class only
while the demand for that class decreases; ``-2`` the next class may
be taken only while its demand increases; ``100 + t``: allowed only
while the cell has had its class for less than ``t`` steps; ``1000 +
t``: allowed only once it has had it for ``t`` steps or more.

Added to the suitability of each cell's own class (CLUE-S's
conversion elasticity, 0 to 1; one value for all, ``{class: value}``
or a list in the class order). Used by the CLUE and CLUMondo
allocations (not by the ordered one, as in lulcc).

Map of restricted cells (``True`` or non-zero: the cell keeps its
class), lulcc's mask with the opposite convention.

Map of the steps each cell has had its class (default 1 everywhere,
as lulcc), updated at each step: +1 where the class stays, 0 where
it changes.

CLUMondo: ``{(from, to): map}``, the conversion code of each cell for
that pair (0 not allowed, 1 allowed, or an age code below).

doc.x:
With the [`CLUMondo`][terraflux.simulate.CLUMondo] allocation the conversion matrix takes
CLUMondo's codes instead: ``1`` allowed, ``0`` not; ``100 + t``: only
once the cell has had its system for ``t`` years; ``-100 - t``: only
until then (the system must leave after ``t`` years when the code is
on the diagonal); ``1000 + t``: autonomous change (succession) after
``t`` years, whatever the demand. ``elasticity`` is CLUMondo's
conversion resistance, ``history`` the starting ages (a map, or a
number: random ages from 1 to it, as CLUMondo draws them).

With CLUMondo, rules may also be given by the role of the transitions
(``roles``, a [`Roles`][terraflux.simulate.Roles]):

- ``allowed`` as ``{role: code}`` (``{"expansion": 0}``; other pairs 1);
- ``transition_resistance``: ``{role or (from, to): value}`` subtracted
  from the score of making that transition;
- ``conversion_order``: roles from the first tried to the last, as a
  resistance of 0.1 per position (``["intensification",
  "expansion"]``: expansion 0.1); ``transition_resistance`` overrides;
- ``caps``: [`Cap`][terraflux.simulate.Cap] limits per year (``Cap("expansion",
  area=...)``);
- ``succession``: [`Succession`][terraflux.simulate.Succession] (autonomous changes).

For each transition and pair of variables, the cross-tabulation of

chi-square, Cramér's V, the contingency coefficient, the joint
entropy (natural logarithms) and the joint information uncertainty

terraflux.stats.name: stats
terraflux.stats.summary: Statistics of maps: trends along series of maps, spatial autocorrelation and interpolation of points.

doc.x:
Computed in C++ with OpenMP, cell by cell, on maps larger than PySAL's and
pymannkendall's loops handle comfortably, with their numbers: the Mann-Kendall
test and Sen's slope of every cell (pymannkendall's ``original_test``, the same
bits), the global and local Moran's I and Getis and Ord's Gi* over the
contiguity of the cells (PySAL's esda, to rounding), and the interpolation of
points onto a map as R's gstat: sample variograms and their fit, inverse
distance weighting, ordinary kriging. The same as Terraflux's ``stats.*``
operators.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    ndvi = tf.load_raster("ndvi_2000_2024.tif")       # a band per year
    t = tf.stats.trend(ndvi)
    t.slope, t.p, t.trend                              # Sen's slope, the test's p, up / down / none

    tf.stats.moran(t.slope)                            # global Moran's I of the slopes
    hot = tf.stats.getis_ord(tf.load_raster("density.tif")).spots

    pts = tf.load_vector("soil_samples.gpkg")          # points with a value
    v = tf.stats.variogram(pts, "carbon", model="exponential")
    k = tf.stats.kriging(pts, dem, v, "carbon")       # onto the cells of a map
    k.prediction, k.variance

point (the system factored once) or the ``nmax`` nearest each cell, and

suitability, the agreement of an ensemble. As Terraflux's

doc.x:
The Mann-Kendall test (S, its variance corrected for ties, z, the two-sided
p, Kendall's tau, increasing or decreasing at ``alpha``) and Sen's slope
(the median of the slopes between every pair of dates, per step of the
series) with its intercept, cell by cell in C++; the missing values of a
cell are left out (a cell with fewer than three values gets NaN).

``tf.load_raster`` reads a multi-band file) or a list of 2-D maps.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
>>> maps = [np.full((2, 2), float(t)) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, (2, 2)) for t in range(10)]
>>> maps = [m * np.array([[1, -1], [0, 1]]) for m in maps]      # up, down, flat, up
>>> t = tf.stats.trend(maps)
>>> t.trend.values.tolist()
[[1.0, -1.0], [0.0, 1.0]]

terraflux.surface.name: surface
terraflux.surface.summary: Surface metrics: the texture of continuous rasters (ISO 25178).

doc.x:
Gradient surface metrics describe a continuous surface (NDVI, elevation,
canopy height...) without classifying it into patches: its amplitude, slopes,
peaks and valleys, the shape of its height distribution, its spatial
autocorrelation and orientation; and terrain indices of DEMs (TPI, TRI, VRM,
curvature, heat load...). Ports of the R packages geodiv (Smith et al. 2021)
and spatialEco (Evans 2021), computed in C++ with OpenMP: their values, bit for
bit where they are right, and the corrected ones where they err.

Typical use::

    import terraflux as tf

    ndvi = tf.surface.example_data("orforest")
    z = tf.surface.remove_plane(ndvi)             # residuals from the trend
    tf.surface.metrics(z)                          # every metric, one table
    tf.surface.sa(z), tf.surface.sku(z)

    width: xr.DataArray | None = None,
)

i:
The ternary pattern: the 8 signs (higher, level, lower) of the
directions as a base-3 number, the smallest of its rotations and
reflections (498 distinct codes, 0 to 6560).

The directions whose zenith angle exceeds the flatness threshold
(whose nadir angle is below minus the threshold), as 8 bits, the
smallest of their rotations (0 to 255).
intensity, exposition, range, variance, elongation, azimuth, extend, width

With ``measures=True``: the mean height of the cell above the points
that decide its directions (``intensity``), minus the height of the
farthest of them in elevation (``exposition``), their range and
variance of elevation; the shape of the octagon they draw on the
plane: its elongation, the azimuth of its long axis (degrees), its
area relative to the octagon of the search radius (``extend``) and
its width (map units).

terraflux.surface._geomorphons.Geomorpho.name: share
terraflux.surface._geomorphons.Geomorpho.summary: Cells and share of each landform: ``form`` (code), ``name``, ``cells``, ``share``.

terraflux.surface._geomorphons.geomorpho.name: geomorphons
terraflux.surface._geomorphons.geomorpho.sig:
geomorphons(
    dem,
    *,
    search: float = 3,
    skip: float = 0,
    flat: float = 1.0,
    dist: float = 0.0,
    units: str = 'cells',
    comparison: str = 'anglev1',
    extended: bool = False,
    measures: bool = False,
    extent=None,
    crs=None,
    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    _grass_errors: bool = False,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> Geomorphons
terraflux.surface._geomorphons.geomorpho.summary: Landforms of a DEM by geomorphons (Jasiewicz & Stepinski 2013).

doc.x:
From each cell, along the 8 directions, the terrain is looked at from
``skip + 1`` cells away up to the search radius: the highest angle above
the horizon (zenith) and the lowest (nadir). A direction is higher (+)
when its zenith angle wins, lower (-) when the nadir angle does, level
when neither exceeds the flatness threshold ``flat``. The numbers of +
and - name the landform (flat, peak, ridge, shoulder, spur, slope,
hollow, footslope, valley, pit), and the 8 signs, up to rotation and
reflection, one of 498 patterns. Unlike slope and curvature, which see a
3 x 3 window, the forms follow the terrain at the scale of the search
radius: a better covariate of the site's shape for land change,
species distributions and soils.

The same forms, patterns and measures as GRASS GIS's ``r.geomorphon``
(8.4), bit for bit, but for four corrections (see Notes).

i:
The DEM (projected; a single band; NaN or ``nodata`` = missing). It is
read as float32, as GRASS reads it.

The outer search radius, in cells (or map units with
``units="map"``): ``r.geomorphon``'s ``search``.
The inner radius not looked at (``skip``), less than ``search``.

The flatness distance (``dist``): beyond it the threshold falls as
the angle of the height ``tan(flat) x dist`` (0: none; it must lie
between ``skip`` and ``search``).

The unit of ``search``, ``skip`` and ``dist`` (``"map"``: map units,
``r.geomorphon -m``).

How the zenith and nadir angles decide a direction
(``r.geomorphon``'s ``comparison``).

The extended correction (``-e``): with a search radius above 10
cells, a ridge, peak, shoulder or footslope is looked at again within
half the radius.

Also the measures of the geomorphon (intensity, exposition, range,
variance, elongation, azimuth, extend, width).

doc.x:
Four things ``r.geomorphon`` 8.4 does not do as intended, here in the
correct form: its lines of sight stop one row short of the DEM's last
row for the cells of its bottom ``search`` rows (a buffer of rows that
holds the last one out of reach); its binary ``positive`` and
``negative`` patterns add the direction numbers instead of setting their
bits; its extended correction keeps the inner radius in the shorter,
second search, though it sets it to 0; and the shape of a geomorphon
whose first direction (NE) has no point is all zeros. Elsewhere the values
are GRASS's, compared on synthetic and real DEMs.

Longitude / latitude DEMs are refused: GRASS measures their distances on
the ellipsoid; reproject the DEM first.

Jasiewicz, J. & Stepinski, T. F. (2013). Geomorphons, a pattern
recognition approach to classification and mapping of landforms.
*Geomorphology* 182, 147-156.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:60, 0:60] * 10.0
>>> hill = 300 * np.exp(-((yy - 300) ** 2 + (xx - 300) ** 2) / 2e4)   # a round hill
>>> g = tf.surface.geomorphons(hill, search=10, extent=(0, 600, 0, 600))
>>> tf.surface.GEOMORPHON_FORMS[int(g.forms[30, 30])]                 # its summit
'peak'
>>> g                                                                  # the hill's flanks: slopes and spurs
Geomorphons(60 x 60; slope 61%, spur 27%, footslope 8%)
>>> g.share().loc[[2, 8], ["name", "cells"]]
           name  cells
form
2          peak     21
8     footslope    274

terraflux.surface._gravity.gravity.name: gravity
terraflux.surface._gravity.gravity.sig:
gravity(
    sources,
    exponent: float = 2.0,
    *,
    mask=None,
    unit: str = 'cells',
    method: str = 'auto',
    extent=None,
    crs=None,
    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> xr.DataArray
terraflux.surface._gravity.gravity.summary: Gravitational interaction potential of source cells.

doc.x:
Every cell gets the sum over the source cells of their mass over the
distance to them raised to ``exponent``: P_i = sum_k m_k / d_ik^beta, the
gravity model of spatial interaction (a "pressure" of towns, markets or
roads to use as a driver of land change). The sources are the cells of
``sources`` with a value (other than 0); the value is the mass. A source's
own cell is at a distance of one cell. This is Dinamica EGO's
``CalcInteractionPotentialMap``.

i: The masses (NaN or ``nodata``: not a source).
The distance decay exponent beta (0: no decay).

A raster on the same grid; the potential is missing where it is
missing. The sources under its missing cells still count.

Distances in cells (Dinamica) or in map units (cell width along
rows, height along columns; a source's own cell at the square root of
the cell area).

``"direct"``: the sum over every source-cell pair, in a fixed order
(the same bits with any thread count); ``"fft"``: the same sum as a
convolution by FFT (rounding errors of about 1e-15 of the largest
term, much faster with many sources); ``"auto"``: direct up to 2000
sources (or 1e8 source-cell pairs).
The potential (float64), 0 where no source reaches (no sources).

doc.x:
Dinamica computes each term and their sum in float32 (relative errors
around 1e-7, growing with the number of sources) and scales the
potential to the range of an integer cell type when asked for one; here
the sum is in float64 and never scaled. Its distances are always in
cells.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> towns = np.full((3, 4), np.nan)
>>> towns[0, 0], towns[2, 3] = 100, 50
>>> p = tf.surface.gravity(towns)
>>> round(float(p[0, 0]), 4), round(float(p[1, 1]), 4)
(103.8462, 60.0)

terraflux.surface._hilltop.Hilltop.sig: Hilltop(app: xr.DataArray, hill: xr.DataArray, hills: pd.DataFrame)

i:

on the DEM, NaN where it has no value.

The id (``hills`` row) of the hill whose upper part holds each cell
(of the highest threshold, where upper parts nest), NaN elsewhere.

One row per summit, highest first: ``x``, ``y`` (the summit), ``top``,
``base``, ``base_kind`` (``"saddle"``: the key col to higher terrain;
``"plain"``: the plain or water body it meets; ``"lowest"``: the lowest
cell of its connected area), ``base_x``, ``base_y`` (the saddle, the
plain cell met, or the lowest cell nearest the summit), ``height``,
``mean_slope`` (degrees, of its cells above the base),
``line_slope`` (degrees, of the line from the summit to its foot: the
nearest cell at or below its base), ``area`` (above the base, map
units squared), ``area_ha`` (hectares; at the centre latitude for
longitude / latitude), ``qualifies``, ``threshold`` (the elevation from which
the APP starts) and ``app_cells``.

terraflux.surface._hilltop.hilltop.name: hilltop
terraflux.surface._hilltop.hilltop.sig:
hilltop(
    dem,
    *,
    min_height: float = 100.0,
    min_slope: float = 25.0,
    slope: str = 'mean',
    fraction: float = 2 / 3,
    plain=None,
    extent=None,
    crs=None,
    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> Hilltop
terraflux.surface._hilltop.hilltop.summary: Hilltops as permanent protection areas (APP de topo de morro).

doc.x:
Brazil's Forest Code (Lei 12.651/2012, art. 4, IX) protects the tops of
hills, mounts, mountains and ranges at least 100 m high and of mean slope
above 25 degrees: the areas above the contour at 2/3 of the height,
measured from the base, which is the plane of the adjacent plain or water
body or, in undulating relief, the elevation of the nearest saddle point.

Every summit of the DEM is found with its base by sweeping the cells from
the highest down and joining each to the regions of its 8 neighbours (a
merge tree): where regions meet, the cell is a saddle, and the regions of
lower summits end there (their base is the saddle: the key col of
topographic prominence, so a range is one elevation above its lowest
saddle and its peaks are hills of their own above theirs). A region that
reaches a cell of ``plain`` gets that cell's elevation as its base; the
highest summit of a connected area that meets neither gets its lowest
elevation. A hill qualifies when its height is at least ``min_height``
and its slope above ``min_slope``; its APP is the area joined to its
summit through cells at least ``base + fraction x height`` high.

i: The DEM (metres), projected or in longitude / latitude.
The least height of a hill (metres; CONAMA 303/2002: 50).

The slope a hill must exceed (degrees; CONAMA 303/2002: about 16.7,
30 %, along the line of steepest slope).

``"mean"``: the mean slope (Horn, degrees) of the hill's cells above
its base (the law's "inclinação média"); ``"line"``: the slope of the
line from the summit to the base cell.
Where the APP starts, as a fraction of the height above the base.

Plains and water bodies (true / non-zero): a hill that reaches them
takes their elevation as its base.

doc.x:
The law leaves room for interpretation and these are the choices made:
the nearest saddle of an elevation is the col where its region meets
higher terrain (the hill's prominence), so the highest peak of a range
is measured from the range's base and lower peaks from their saddles;
the mean slope is that of the cells of the hill above its base (its
region in the merge tree); the APP is the part of that region above the
threshold that is joined to the summit (a separate peak above the
threshold, joined below it, is judged as a hill of its own). Plains are
not inferred from the slope: give ``plain`` (flat floodplains, lakes,
rivers, the sea). Cells on the DEM's edges have no slope and are left out
of the mean. Results depend on the DEM's resolution and accuracy, and
automatic delineation is a starting point for field and legal work.

Dinamica EGO's ``CalcHilltop`` follows CONAMA 303/2002 on a DEM cut into
elevation bands: bases are the band of a local minimum reached
downhill, and its slope criterion is the angle between the summit and
the nearest cell of the base band that borders other features or the
map's edge (5 degrees for an isolated cone of 21.8 degrees in a plain,
measured with Dinamica EGO 8.13), so its results differ.

i:
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:100, 0:100] * 10.0
>>> cone = 500 + np.clip(300 - 1.0 * np.hypot(yy - 500, xx - 500), 0, None)  # 300 m high, 45 degrees
>>> h = tf.surface.hilltop(cone, extent=(0, 1000, 0, 1000))
>>> top = h.hills.iloc[0]
>>> float(top.base), float(top.height), round(float(top.mean_slope)), bool(top.qualifies)
(500.0, 300.0, 44, True)
>>> int(np.nansum(h.app)) == int(np.sum(cone >= 700))   # the APP: above 500 + 2/3 x 300
True

terraflux.surface._plane.best_fit_plane.summary: The polynomial surface of order 0 to 3 that fits a surface best.

doc.x:
Of the four least-squares surfaces (`fit_plane()`), the one with the
least Bayesian information criterion, N log(RSS / N) + p log(N) (N cells
with a value, p coefficients), the lowest order on ties. The order is in
``attrs["order"]``.

geodiv's ``bestfitplane`` takes the smallest absolute mean residual, but
every least-squares fit with a constant term has residuals that average to
zero: its choice rests on rounding errors (about 1e-17). To remove a trend
of a chosen order, subtract `fit_plane()`.

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> ndvi = tf.surface.example_data("orforest")
>>> tf.surface.best_fit_plane(ndvi).attrs["order"]
2

>>> import terraflux as tf

As geodiv: the surface times a two-dimensional Hann window, its power
spectrum by FFT, the inverse FFT of that, shifted to put zero lag in the
centre and divided by its maximum. With missing cells, the largest square
without them around the centre is used (and the image covers it).

terraflux.surface._spatial.scl.sig:
scl(
    x,
    threshold=THRESHOLDS,

    extent=None,

    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray
terraflux.surface._spatial.scl.summary: Correlation lengths: how far the autocorrelation takes to decay.

doc.x:
On the upper half of `aacf()` (with the zero-lag row), the distances
(map units; metres on longitude/latitude rasters) from zero lag to the
cells whose autocorrelation is at or below each threshold: the shortest
(fastest decay, Sal for 0.2) and the longest (slowest decay).

i: The fastest decay length for each threshold, then the slowest ones.

doc.x:
Distances are exact in map units on projected rasters and haversine
distances (terra's, radius 6378137 m) on longitude/latitude ones. geodiv
measures from one row above zero lag (its upper half leaves that row out),
with GDAL's proximity in single precision and the cell width in both
directions, and fails with missing cells.

    nodata=None,

terraflux.surface._spatial.sfd.summary: Fractal dimension of the surface (Sfd), by triangular prisms.

doc.x:
Clarke's (1986) method as geodiv implements it: heights rescaled to 0-1,
the area of triangular prisms over the central square of a power-of-two
side at cell sizes 1, 2, 4...; 2 minus the slope of log(area) against
log(cell area). geodiv's code has a typo in one prism side, rescales
against 99999 / -99999 when the heights exceed them and reads past the
raster (1-based indices): corrected here.

terraflux.surface._spatial.srw.name: srw
terraflux.surface._spatial.srw.sig:
srw(

    *,
    extent=None,
    crs=None,
    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray
terraflux.surface._spatial.srw.summary: Dominant radial wavelength (Srw), its index (Srwi) and the half-power wavelength (Shw).

doc.x:
The amplitude of the surface's Fourier spectrum (upper half) summed over
circles around zero frequency (up to 100, evenly spaced): Srw is the
radius with the largest sum, Srwi the mean sum over the largest, Shw the
radius that splits the summed amplitude in half (NaN on ties), measured
from zero frequency (geodiv: from one row above it). Radii are distances in
the spectrum in map units: a texture repeating k times across a raster of
n cells has its peak at k cell sizes, a wavelength of n / k cells.

terraflux.surface._spatial.std.name: std
terraflux.surface._spatial.std.sig:
std(
    x,
    *,
    extent=None,
    crs=None,
    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray
terraflux.surface._spatial.std.summary: Texture direction (Std) and texture direction index (Stdi).

doc.x:
From the amplitude of the surface's Fourier spectrum (upper half, within
the largest circle around zero frequency that fits), summed over
orientations 0 to 179.5 degrees in steps of 0.5 (+-0.25): Std is
the angle with the largest sum, Stdi the mean sum over the largest (near
1: no dominant direction). Angles are those of the frequency vector: 0 for
a texture that varies along x (stripes running north-south), 90 for one
that varies along y.

geodiv takes the angles from one row above and, on even widths, one column
left of zero frequency, and includes zero frequency (the sum of the
heights) in the 0 degree bin.

terraflux.surface._terrain.curvature.name: curvature
terraflux.surface._terrain.curvature.sig:
curvature(
    x,
    type: str = 'planform',
    *,
    extent=None,
    crs=None,
    band=None,
    nodata=None,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
) -> xr.DataArray

doc.x:
``"planform"``, ``"profile"`` and ``"total"`` (their sum) from Zevenbergen
& Thorne's (1987) partial derivatives of the 3 x 3 neighbourhood, p, q
(first) and r, s, t (second): planform -(q^2 r - 2pqs + p^2 t) /
((p^2 + q^2) sqrt(1 + p^2 + q^2)), profile -(p^2 r + 2pqs + q^2 t) /
((p^2 + q^2) (1 + p^2 + q^2)^(3/2)); ``"mcnab"``: the mean of the
differences between the cell and its 8 neighbours, divided by its largest
value; ``"bolstad"``: 10000 (z - mean of the 3 x 3) / 1000 / (1.5 cell
width).

i: The DEM, on a projected raster (see `terrain()`).

Missing on the edges (and flat cells for the Zevenbergen & Thorne
curvatures).

doc.x:
spatialEco halves the second derivatives (divides by 2 L^2), pads the
edges with 0, rounds to 6 decimals, uses the cell width for both
directions, divides McNab's sum by 9 and subtracts 1 (operator
precedence), and fails for ``"bolstad"``: corrected here.

i:
>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> c = tf.surface.curvature(tf.surface.example_data("normforest"), "total")
>>> c.shape
(371, 371)

Their equations 1-3 of potential direct incident radiation from slope,
folded aspect and latitude: the aspect folded about the northeast-southwest
line (hottest on southwest slopes; southern hemisphere: about northwest-
southeast) or, with ``direct``, about north-south. The equations give the

terraflux.surface._terrain.tpi.summary: Topographic position index: the elevation minus the mean of the window.

doc.x:
Positive on ridges and hilltops, negative in valleys, near 0 on flats and
even slopes. The window includes the cell itself; cells whose window
reaches a missing cell or the edge are missing.

i:
``"rectangle"``: the window's side in cells (odd); ``"circle"``: its
radius in map units (at least two cells).
Divided by the window's standard deviation.

sums along the rows, one step per window row: within about 1e-13 of the
values' range of summing each window.

``normalize``, a standard deviation of 0 by a misplaced parenthesis): it
is not offered.

>>> import terraflux as tf
>>> dem = tf.surface.example_data("orelevation")

terraflux.surface._viewshed.viewshed.sig:
viewshed(
    dem,
    observers,
    *,
